<kanji>Lead</kanji> <kanji>poison</kanji> is <vocabulary>lead toxicity</vocabulary>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>times</radical>.

readingMnemonic: The readings come from the vocab words 見る and 送る. Make sure you know those and you'll know this word's reading as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

When a vocab is a single kanji with okurigana, chances are it's going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you don't usually learn in the kanji (you usually learn the on'yomi reading). So, let's learn the kun'yomi reading for this word using its meaning.

This word may be hard to understand at first, but there are many things the Japanese consider to be Japanese-only. These theories range from reasonable to ridiculous, but either way, you'll see them described as 日本的.

readingMnemonic: The readings come from 甲斐 and 生き, so if you know those you may have a <vocabulary>reason for living</vocabulary>, or at least a reason for doing your kanji study. Be careful of the rendaku changing 甲斐's reading to がい!
meaningMnemonic:
You know that 生きる is "to live" and 甲斐 is "effect" or "worth." Something that has a good effect on your life and gives it worth is your <vocabulary>reason for living</vocabulary>. From your standpoint, it's <vocabulary>something worth living for</vocabulary>.

Keep in mind 生き甲斐 is mostly used as a noun, so you'll see it in phrases like 仕事が生き甲斐 (my job is my reason for living) or 生き甲斐が欲しい (I want something to live for).

readingMnemonic: Remember that 1 ton weight? Well, actually it’s a <reading>dou</reading>ghnut (どう). A huge, massive, 1 ton doughnut. It’s super heavy and hard to move, but it’s delicious.

readingMnemonic: You use the word <kanji>I</kanji> a lot. You say it so much, you just start referring to yourself with the french <reading>beaucoup</reading> (ぼく) for a lot. Because you love yourself a lot.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> of <radical>business</radical>? Ha! That's <kanji>me</kanji>! That's <kanji>I</kanji>!

readingMnemonic: Since this is an alternate version of 柔らかい, it has the same reading too. If you remember that, you can remember this word's reading.
meaningMnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. The kanji means <kanji>soft</kanji>, so the adjective form of that is exactly the same: <vocabulary>soft</vocabulary>.

While 柔らかい describes a pleasant, gentle softness or graceful flexibility, 軟らかい refers to softness or pliability as an objective physical property. So, for example, 柔らかいお肉 is the delicious, tender steak you have at a fancy restaurant, while 軟らかいお肉 simply describes the only kind of meat your toothless granny can eat. Likewise, a graceful gymnast or ballerina has a 柔らかい体, while your friend who can fit himself inside a suitcase — well, he has an objectively 軟らかい体.

This is used particularly when referring to waka poetry.

Later that evening, you see no shrimp, just ice. The supply of shrimp has been <kanji>exhaust</kanji>ed. It's all gone! You never thought they'd <kanji>use up</kanji> their shrimp supply so quickly.

This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned the on'yomi reading for 袖, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

It's always hard to fill a <vocabulary>leader</vocabulary>s' <reading>shoe</reading>s (しゅう). Leaders have big responsibilities and power. Just big shoes to fill! Picture these big ol' leader's shoes, like in a literal sense. Not only do they have big responsibilities, leaders have big shoes as well.

Someone who has <kanji>territory</kanji> under their <kanji>sleeve</kanji> is the <vocabulary>leader</vocabulary>. They're the <vocabulary>boss</vocabulary> of all this territory because they say so, and because they shoved it all into their big sleeves.

This is a very formal word often used in political contexts, particularly when referring to the leader of a faction or political party.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!
meaningMnemonic:
You've seen how 変える means "to change" something. This word means that something changed by itself, so it means <vocabulary>to be changed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be altered</vocabulary>.

変わる refers to the act of changing into something different, and involves alterations in nature, appearance, or state. For example, it can describe changes in weather or the season, someone undergoing a noticeable change in appearance or behavior, or one's feelings or thoughts evolving over time.

Since 変わる means "becoming something different," you can also use 変わった and 変わっている to describe someone or something that's "different from what's normal." For example, you can say 変わった人 or 変わっている人 to mean "an odd person."

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

The kanji and the radical that look like this are exactly the same. They are both <kanji>Asia</kanji>. 

This can also mean <kanji>sub-</kanji>. As in subtropics, subspecies, subhuman… That kind of sub-! When it's not in a place name, 亜 will usually be using its sub- meaning.

So when you see this radical, think of all the different ceremonies you might have to go to in your life and what you'll need to wear.

Remember 足りる? That is "to be enough." How can you make something be enough? You keep adding things to the pile until you reach that point where there are enough! That's why this verb is <vocabulary>to add something</vocabulary>, because you keep adding things until you 足りる.

This verb is transitive, like most verbs ending in す, which is why you are adding something. It's not getting itself added all by itself. Maybe you add so much that someone tries to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you for that nasty pile of squirrels you keep outside.

meaningMnemonic: 払い is a "payment" and 戻す is "to return." If you return a payment, you are going <vocabulary>to repay</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to refund</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to reimburse</vocabulary> someone for their payment.

A 棋院 is an organizational body for professional and amateur go players. It puts on tournaments, assigns rankings, and even hosts actual matches sometimes, which is why this can also be translated as a <vocabulary>go hall</vocabulary> in some contexts.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

meaningMnemonic: When you take the <kanji>whole</kanji> and <kanji>join</kanji> it together, you get a <vocabulary>synthesis</vocabulary>, and probably a good <vocabulary>overall</vocabulary> picture of things.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Cow</kanji> <kanji>milk</kanji> is <vocabulary>cow's milk</vocabulary>, though most people just call cow's milk <vocabulary>milk</vocabulary>.

meaningMnemonic: It <kanji>revolve</kanji>s then <kanji>capsize</kanji>s. When a ship revolves onto its back and then capsizes, this causes <vocabulary>capsizing</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
You have to remember the た portion of this word to learn the reading of it. Think of it this way:

You have <vocabulary>to stand up</vocabulary> in order to wave goodbye to someone. When you stand up, you also say <reading>ta</reading>-ta (た)!
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "stand" so what is the verb version of that? It's <vocabulary>to stand</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The reading for 画 is the secondary reading though (かく), so take note of that.
meaningMnemonic:
Take your <kanji>plan</kanji> and add some <kanji>image</kanji>s to it. This is your <vocabulary>plan</vocabulary>.

While 計画 refers to plans in general, 企画 specifically refers to the planning of events, projects, or initiatives, as well as the actual projects being planned.

readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the word 陰. <vocabulary>Thanks to</vocabulary> that other vocab word, you can read this one!
meaningMnemonic:
陰 is a shadow, and adding お to it and makes it honorific. It becomes the shadow of someone very important, and means <vocabulary>thanks to</vocabulary>, as in "thanks to you, I was able to pass the test." This originally comes from the idea of being in the shadow of the gods, who are protecting you and helping you out!

If that's hard to remember, think about shade helping you out. Perhaps <vocabulary>thanks to</vocabulary> the <kanji>shade</kanji> you were able to survive the heat of the desert.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Be sure to omit the 〜 in your answer as it is only a placeholder for a number.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: This <kanji>achievement</kanji> was made possible by <reading>こう</reading>いち, so of course this construction project is a giant statue of the man himself. What an achievement of a statue. What an achievement of an achievement.
meaningMnemonic: Using your <radical>construction</radical> <radical>power</radical> you build something great. A true <kanji>achievement</kanji> built for the achievement of making kanji learning easier!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Sew</kanji> to <kanji>manufacture</kanji> things by <vocabulary>sewing</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: An <kanji>especially</kanji> <kanji>special</kanji> thing is even more <vocabulary>special</vocabulary> and probably a lot more <vocabulary>unique</vocabulary> than ordinary special things.

readingMnemonic:

Just think about the <vocabulary>train direction</vocabulary> that <reading>you</reading> (ゆ) need to go in. It's all about you. Not your friends or anyone else. You. You are the most important person at this train station.
meaningMnemonic: This is a weird word. Call it exceptional. You'll see this at train stations, especially. You know the kanji means <kanji>go</kanji>. So, something is going somewhere. Now just use the き to help you to remember that this word means <vocabulary>train direction</vocabulary> (aka it tells you which direction a train is going), because this word is the key (き) to you knowing what direction you're going in so you don't get lost. You could also remember this word as "<vocabulary>bound for</vocabulary>" aka "Bound for Tokyo Station."

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Be careful of the ねっ portion (normally is ねつ).
meaningMnemonic: When your <kanji>heart</kanji> is <kanji>fever</kanji>ish and hot about something, it is obviously something you have a lot of <vocabulary>enthusiasm</vocabulary> about. Think about the things you've enthusiasm for. Then, imagine your heart beating and getting all hot from thinking about it. Why else would people get so upset when talking about religion and politics. It's their feverish heart! Their enthusiasm!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned the readings for both of these kanji, so you should be able to read this word already!

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Note that for the word fence in Japanese, フェンス is typically used. 垣 isn't very common but it's sometimes used in literature.

You and your friends grab some <reading>bats</reading> (ばつ) and use these bats to beat the drunkard leader. Being beaten with bats frightens him, and he scurries away.
meaningMnemonic: Passed out in front of your <radical>gate</radical> lies a former <radical>leader</radical>. He's now a <radical>drunkard</radical>, but once ran a popular <kanji>clique</kanji> called the Cool Kids <kanji>Clan</kanji>. The clan has fallen apart, and he no longer has a clique to call his own.

Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

What did you just <vocabulary>win</vocabulary>? You won a new <reading>ca</reading>r (か)!

You <kanji>explode</kanji> with <kanji>laugh</kanji>s. Wow, what <vocabulary>explosive laughter</vocabulary>.

爆笑 means to <vocabulary>burst out laughing</vocabulary>, often loudly and uncontrollably. While it originally referred to group laughter, it can now also be used by and for individuals. You can even use it like <vocabulary>LOL</vocabulary> or LMAO in English: just stick it at the end of your Japanese messages to show you're really laughing it up.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading when you learned 偏る, so you should be able to read this one too!
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>child</kanji> of a <kanji>judge</kanji> is the thing he puts on his judgements. What does he put on his judgments? His <vocabulary>seal</vocabulary>, you know, to make it all official and stuff.

meaningMnemonic: If 暮らす is "to live" or "to live one's life," then to live one's life as 一人, means you are <vocabulary>living alone</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: You want to <kanji>sue</kanji> them back so you clean the axe with some <reading>so</reading>ap (そ). "Your honor," you say in court, "I don't see any drops of blood, I countersue!"

You hit someone with that axe and now they're going to <kanji>sue</kanji> you. That drop of blood on your axe is pretty incriminating, which is why they have enough of a case to sue you.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>guy</radical>.
Remember how words beginning with ど are often question words, and words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception, so どこ means <vocabulary>where</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is just the kun'yomi reading you learned with 元, but twice, so you should be good to go!
meaningMnemonic:
It's the <kanji>origin</kanji> of all <kanji>origin</kanji>s, so it's the way it was <vocabulary>originally</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>from the beginning</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>by nature</vocabulary>. You get the idea.

Note that this is frequently written in just hiragana, but you'll encounter the kanji version too!

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is put on the end of numbers to show how old someone is.

You already learned 〜才 (years old), and 〜歳 means the exact same thing. No trick questions here. The difference is that 歳 is a pretty complicated kanji, so 才 is the simplified, more casual option for easier readability. Basically, 才 is the jeans-and-t-shirt version, while 歳 shows up in a suit and tie when things get official.

readingMnemonic: The reading for 興奮 is one you didn't learn with the kanji, though it's similar. Instead of きょう it's こう, so just think of how whenever you feel excitement, it's thanks to <reading>こう</reading>いち. So just think of こういち exciting you in some way to remember this vocab's reading.
meaningMnemonic: My <kanji>interest</kanji> is <kanji>stirred up</kanji>! I'm feeling <vocabulary>excitement</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>stimulation</vocabulary> from all this stirring up, in fact!

readingMnemonic: If you know the kun'yomi readings of both of these kanji you should be okay. You have two separate single-kanji words put together by a の. That's why it's the kun'yomi reading - they're separate.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>man</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is a <vocabulary>boy</vocabulary>.

There's a の particle stuck in the middle of this word. Here it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after. 

But for now, all you really have to remember is that 男の子 means "boy."

readingMnemonic: As the tsunami comes to <kanji>sink</kanji> the pirate, the pirate holds his <reading>chin</reading> (ちん) up high. He will die with dignity.
meaningMnemonic: If a <radical>tsunami</radical> hits a <radical>pirate</radical> they are going to <kanji>sink</kanji> no matter how good of a pirate captain they are.

readingMnemonic: How do you know someone is a <vocabulary>royal consort</vocabulary>? Because they <reading>kiss a ki</reading>ng (きさき). If you kiss a king, maybe you can be a royal consort too!
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the vocabulary are exactly the same, so this means <vocabulary>royal consort</vocabulary>. Depending on who she's married to, she could be a <vocabulary>queen</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>princess</vocabulary>, or even an <vocabulary>empress</vocabulary>. 

妃 can overlap in meaning with 后, but 后 is reserved for the highest-ranking consort, like an empress or queen, while 妃 is a more general word which includes lower-ranking consorts and the wives of other royal family members. In modern Japanese, the kana version きさき often appears in fairytale-style stories with kings and queens. But it's good to know both kanji, especially if you're reading anything historical.

readingMnemonic:
The reading is a strange one, different from anything you've learned, kanji on'yomi or vocab kun'yomi. The reading is この, so think of this: 

What’s something easy <vocabulary>to be fond of</vocabulary>? <reading>子</reading>? <reading>No</reading> (この), not for you. You’re always saying “子? No!” Most people are fond of kids, at least their own, but not you. Noisy, germy, needy 子? No, no thank you!
meaningMnemonic: You know that 好き is "like." Although 好き is kind of like a verb already, this is definitely a verb. It can be <vocabulary>to be fond of</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to like</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

<vocabulary>Long ago</vocabulary>, in a galaxy far away, a bunch of prequel movies were ruined by a single character. "<reading>Heesa</reading> (ひさ) the best character!" you hear. Oh no. Heesa here. Get out before Jar Jar Binks gets you! Keep him in the past!
meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with しい on the end, meaning it's an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>long time</kanji>? Well, it's <vocabulary>long ago</vocabulary>, or can mean <vocabulary>for a long time</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The thing you <kanji>extract</kanji> from a <kanji>phenomenon</kanji> is an <vocabulary>abstraction</vocabulary>. Extracting abstraction out of a phenomenon may not sound like a very concrete or vivid mnemonic, but I guess that makes it an appropriate abstraction…

readingMnemonic: You touch the <kanji>paint</kanji> in the dirt with your <reading>toe</reading> (と) to see if it's still wet. It is. The paint is still very wet and now your toe looks like a tiny rainbow.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> <radical>surplus</radical> will cover all the <radical>dirt</radical> with <kanji>paint</kanji>. The surplus of tsunamis will strike the paint factories first (everyone knows paint factories are built close to the ocean). Then the paint will flow over all the dirt and paint it a ton of rainbow colors.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Something <kanji>normal</kanji> and <kanji>universal</kanji> is still <vocabulary>universal</vocabulary>. Normally.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>place</kanji> you have <kanji>control</kanji> over is your <vocabulary>jurisdiction</vocabulary>.

所轄 commonly refers to the jurisdiction of a police station or other law enforcement agency, like 所轄の警察署 (the district police station) or 所轄の税務署 (the district tax office). It can also be used for government departments that have authority over certain tasks or regions, like 所轄官庁 (the authorities concerned), as well as within organizations to describe which department is responsible for specific tasks, like 所轄部門 (the responsible department).

readingMnemonic: The reading for the kanji portion uses the kun'yomi reading. This is kind of like the reading you already learned for 形 just without the ち part. And rendaku happens too, so it becomes がた. If you can remember that, you should be able to remember this reading too!
meaningMnemonic:
ハート is of course "heart" and you know that 形 means <kanji>shape</kanji>. You've probably already figured this one out. It's <vocabulary>heart shaped</vocabulary>. 

You can add this kanji to all sorts of other things too to say "____ shaped." Give it a try!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>warm</kanji> <kanji>degree</kanji>s is how many degrees warm it is in here. Of course, there can be very few warm degrees as well, making it very cold. What is all this? It's the <vocabulary>temperature</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Not wanting to end up dead in enemy <kanji>territory</kanji>, you decide to escape this geoduck leader by getting on a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and rowing your way outta there. The geoduck commander orders you to halt your escape, but you still get in your row boat and row away.
meaningMnemonic: Taking <radical>orders</radical> from a <radical>geoduck</radical> will place you into enemy <kanji>territory</kanji>. Geoducks make terrible commanders, so if you take orders from one, expect to end up in unknown territory, potentially even enemy territory. Be prepared.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this makes no sense at all. You'll have to learn it straight up, that is, unless you know the word おいしい already, which many people do as it's used in every other sentence in every Japanese variety show. If you don't know this word already, just think of yourself eating something <vocabulary>delicious</vocabulary>. It's so delicious it makes you mad, I have no idea why. You yell at the chef: "<reading>OI</reading> (おい). OI! WHY IS THIS SO DELICIOUS????"
meaningMnemonic:
Something with a <kanji>beauty</kanji> <kanji>taste</kanji> is something that is really <vocabulary>tasty</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>delicious</vocabulary>. Mmmm, yum!

While 美味しい mostly describes tasty food, you may also occasionally see it being used for a sweet deal or situation that benefits you.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: 

A <vocabulary>beast</vocabulary>... what do you think of when you think of a beast? How about a thing (物, もの) full of fur (毛, け), aka a けもの (fur thing)? A beast is a fur thing, and in Japanese that's けもの. Punnnns.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: The か of 神 is used here (losing the み). Then, everything else should be self explanatory.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>god</kanji> <kanji>Nara</kanji> <kanji>river</kanji> <kanji>Prefecture</kanji> is <vocabulary>Kanagawa Prefecture</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>bad</kanji> <kanji>woman</kanji> is an <vocabulary>evil woman</vocabulary>. Surprisingly, "mother in law" is not one of the meanings for this word.

readingMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached, so you can bet it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn this reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're at a baseball game watching people <vocabulary>throw</vocabulary> balls around. But you're hungry so you call for a snack from a vendor. readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word:

What comes off of <vocabulary>fire</vocabulary>? Lots and lots of <reading>hea</reading>t (ひ). Feel it coming off the fire, touching and warming your face.
meaningMnemonic: This vocab is made from a single kanji, which means it shares the same meaning as the parent kanji: <vocabulary>fire</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 稼ぐ.

meaningMnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> with a <radical>spoon</radical> is a powerful thing. Even something as ordinary as a spoon can create great <kanji>change</kanji> in the world when given to the right person.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading is the same as 降参 as well, of course.
meaningMnemonic: 降参 is "surrender" so the verb version would be <vocabulary>to surrender</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>savings</kanji> <kanji>gold</kanji> is your <vocabulary>savings</vocabulary>. You'd be good to have gold right now in your savings, actually. Melt it down into bars, manngggg.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out for the rendaku.
meaningMnemonic:
*Ahem.* This is the <kanji>convenience</kanji> <kanji>facility</kanji>. What place above all others should be convenient to get to? You know, just in case? That would be the <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary>. You might also call it the <vocabulary>bathroom</vocabulary>, the <vocabulary>toilet</vocabulary>, the lavatory, or the facilities.

This word is casual and can often sound gruff, so you won't normally see it on official signs or hear it in polite conversation. It's worth knowing so you can understand it in casual speaking and writing though.

readingMnemonic: This combines the on'yomi readings in the 土俵 vocab with the kun'yomi reading you learned from the 際 vocab. Just think of these as two familiar vocab words mashed together and you should be good to go!

readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>collar</kanji> has "<reading>Eri</reading>c" (えり) emblazoned on it in cursive letters, because this is the stage name you use when you do your lumberjack act. Eric's not your real name, of course — you just think it sounds hunky and looks good on a collar.
meaningMnemonic: What <radical>outfit</radical> do you wear when cutting down <radical>tree</radical>s with a <radical>jackhammer</radical>? A <kanji>collar</kanji>. Yup, just a collar… plus some shirt cuffs and slacks, of course. You know, the classic Chippendales look.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>leave behind</kanji> <kanji>property</kanji> it's known as your <vocabulary>inheritance</vocabulary>.

meaningMnemonic: Someone or something whose 由緒 (lineage) is 正しい (correct) is <vocabulary>of honorable lineage</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>venerable</vocabulary> indeed.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this already!
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Throat</kanji> <kanji>candy</kanji> is the kind of candy that should make your throat feel better. That's right, it's a <vocabulary>cough drop</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>throat lozenge</vocabulary>. Don't just eat regular candy when your throat hurts! Use the right kind.

readingMnemonic: You should be able to figure out the reading from learning 代わる in the previous level.

This is very similar in meaning to 越える. Both can refer to overcoming some physical object or passing beyond a certain amount of time. You're going <vocabulary>to dangle something</vocabulary>, but what? You're going to dangle a <reading>ta</reading>co (た) in front of a hungry person. Kind of a jerk move, honestly. You'll also probably end up dribbling taco sauce all over their shirt, which will earn you double jerk points.

You can remember it's transitive because of the す ending, which you've seen with lots of transitive verbs by now.

垂らす describes when you dangle something or let something hang in a way which allows gravity to act on it, like hanging a line when fishing. It's also used to describe letting something drip — for example, a little kid letting mucus drip from their nose or a sleeping person dribbling drool out of their mouth.

It's not first because it's the best or anything — you love all your eyeballs equally, after all — but it does happen to come first in sequence in your display right now.

The kanji isn't used too often for this word, so just use the kana when you write it. But you'll see the kanji used sometimes, so it's important to be able to recognize it!

Even if you blabber on with your big mouth, as long as everyone knows that your heart is filled with kindness, they will love and accept you.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>first</kanji> <kanji>edition</kanji> is the <vocabulary>first edition</vocabulary>.

meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Go upstream</kanji> through the currents of time to <kanji>reach</kanji> something in the past — this is called <vocabulary>being retroactive</vocabulary>. 

遡及 is a formal, technical word used when something is applied retroactively. You'll mostly see it in legal or administrative contexts when discussing rules or effects that are being applied to past actions or situations.

readingMnemonic: Your favorite Chinese thing to do is <reading>tan</reading> (たん). You can wander around without your shirt on and tan all day. No one will <kanji>sigh</kanji> or scoff at you, it’s perfectly acceptable. The Chinese just love to get their tan on.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>truth</kanji> is that you <kanji>exist</kanji> in <vocabulary>reality</vocabulary>. This is your <vocabulary>real existence</vocabulary>. Well, that makes sense, I suppose.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A beforehand measure is when you make a prediction or estimation about something. While 予想 often refers to a subjective prediction, 予測 generally refers to forecasting future events based on objective evidence.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

When we need to remember the reading しゃ, we use "shaman".

There's a <kanji>car</kanji>. It's the nicest car you've ever seen. Exquisite, beautiful. Wouldn't you be surprised to learn it belongs to a <reading>sha</reading>man (しゃ)? Well it does. This shaman charges a premium for his shaman services so he can afford fancy cars like this.
meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>car</radical> and the kanji <kanji>car</kanji> are exactly the same.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out for the ひ becoming a び like it did in the word 曜日.
meaningMnemonic: This is a day of the week. You know this because it has 曜日 in it. But what day of the week is it? The <kanji>Sun</kanji> day of the week is <vocabulary>Sunday</vocabulary>. Doesn't get much easier than that for you. Lucky!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Something that is <kanji>pure</kanji> <kanji>fur</kanji> is pure fur... but what kind of fur? In this case it's wool, making this mean <vocabulary>all wool</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji reading you learned, probably because this is stuck onto things, describing various squads.
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

隊 is commonly used as a suffix to refer to an organized group or unit, often one that works together toward a specific goal or purpose, like a レスキュー隊 (rescue <vocabulary>squad</vocabulary>), 軍の部隊 (military <vocabulary>unit</vocabulary>), or 登山隊 (mountaineering <vocabulary>team</vocabulary>)!

readingMnemonic: The reading can come from 絶つ, so as long as you know that word you know this one as well.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>die out</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to die out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to come to an end</vocabulary>.

絶える is mostly used for when something that was ongoing comes to an end, like breath stopping, laughter fading away, a supply being cut off, or foot traffic dying down. You know this because when something dies out, nothing is left but thin air (える).

readingMnemonic: The reading is totally an exception. The reading comes from the meaning, though. Yukata = ゆかた.

The <kanji>bathe</kanji> <kanji>clothes</kanji> are clothes you wear to and from the bath. They're your <vocabulary>yukata</vocabulary>.

浴衣 originated as robes worn in a steam bath (that explains the kanji), but these days people mostly wear them at summer festivals or traditional Japanese inns. Be careful not to mix up 浴衣 with 着物, which are much more formal and elaborate!

readingMnemonic:
Sometimes kanji have exceptional readings that are neither on'yomi nor kun'yomi, and this is one of them. So here's a mnemonic to help you remember this reading:

If you're <vocabulary>unskillful</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>bad at</vocabulary> something and you complain about it, then you're just a <reading>hater</reading> (へた). Don't be a hater; get better.

Everything <kanji>below</kanji> that <kanji>hand</kanji> equals <vocabulary>unskillful</vocabulary>. That's why "below hand" means <vocabulary>unskilled</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>bad at</vocabulary>!

She is not happy that you're stretching her things. You should probably try to un-stretch it, put it down, and run before she beats you.
meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>bow</radical> and you want to make it <radical>long</radical>. To do that, you'd naturally just <kanji>stretch</kanji> it.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>attach</radical>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>insert</kanji> and <kanji>enter</kanji> something, you are doing <vocabulary>insertion</vocabulary> to it.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this word can come from level 14 item 残る. Associate the two in your mind and you'll be able to read both.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>remainder</kanji>, but you can't really "to remainder." What is something that's similar that would make sense? How about <vocabulary>to leave behind</vocabulary>. This is when you're actually doing the leaving behind too. For example, you eat some food and you leave behind your rice because you're a bad child. You can remember this because of す. Every time you leave some food behind your mom would <reading>sue</reading> you, because she was a terrible mom. Imagine this.

焦がす means to burn the surface of something, usually blackening it to some degree. Unlike 焦げる, it can be for both intentional burning (a nice crème brûlée) and accidental burning (leaving bread in the toaster too long, scorching your sleeve on the stove).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: You remember 提案, which means <kanji>proposition</kanji>? Make that into a verb and you have <vocabulary>to propose</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>doubt</kanji> <kanji>problem</kanji> is caused by having too much <vocabulary>doubt</vocabulary>. Just think about it. Don't doubt yourself, it's why you're getting those vocab words wrong! :P

meaningMnemonic:
駆ける is "to gallop" and the kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>. To gallop into a place is <vocabulary>to rush into</vocabulary> it. You can’t gallop slowly, after all.

This can also mean <vocabulary>to seek refuge</vocabulary>, as in hurrying to a place for safety and support.
This looks just like a folding <radical>stool</radical>, am I right?

I am going <vocabulary>to obey</vocabulary> you. I think your order is a bit of <reading>shit が</reading> (したが), I'll do it and obey you.

This turkey is trying to escape from Wolverine by leaping over a fence. Wolverine doesn’t want the turkey to escape, but you kick him with your foot and the turkey is then free to leap to safety.

readingMnemonic: You are so <kanji>noisy</kanji> and loud that the townsfolk hired <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the Samurai to shut you up.

meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>fish</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fish shop</vocabulary>, a place from which you buy fish. Especially in Japan, very important.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>simple</kanji> bits of <kanji>language</kanji> are the individual <vocabulary>word</vocabulary>s. If you think about it, this is true. First of all, there are a ton of them. Second, they're tiny. They're just little bits of language and the "word" for these little bits is <vocabulary>word</vocabulary>.

So what’s the difference between this and 言葉? Well, 言葉 can cover any meaningful set of words – anything from words, sentences and paragraphs, to whole texts and even languages. 単語, on the other hand, is a subset of 言葉 that specifically refers to single, distinct words.

readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

If something is the <kanji>latter</kanji>, it can't be first, it has to be at least <vocabulary>second</vocabulary>. This works for lists too. So if you have A through D, it's going to be <vocabulary>B</vocabulary>.

This word is also used as slang for おつかれさま, which is where the <vocabulary>thanks</vocabulary> meaning comes from. It can also be used as a prefix to mean <vocabulary>chic</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Because the rake is persistently <kanji>resistant</kanji>, you eventually tie it to the table with your neck <reading>tie</reading> (たい). The tie won’t hold for long, so you need to take each measurement quickly.
meaningMnemonic: You take a <radical>rake</radical> in for a <radical>measurement</radical> but it is <kanji>resistant</kanji>. The rake doesn’t want to have its measurements taken. The rake is resistant to have any measurement taken because it feels inferior to the other rakes and doesn’t want to be embarrassed if it ends up being smaller than the others.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>land</kanji> is the biggest types of land on this earth that there are. That is a <vocabulary>continent</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 湿る.

Note that this is a formal word that's commonly used in professional or official contexts.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>sigh</kanji> <kanji>breath</kanji> is a <vocabulary>sigh</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings. Since you didn't learn that reading for 粉 with the kanji, here's a mnemonic to help you out. What sort of people like <vocabulary>wheat flour</vocabulary> the most? <reading>子</reading>! 子 like wheat flour the most since it is both fun to eat and to play with. Silly 子, wheat flour is a food, not a toy.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Wheat</kanji> <kanji>powder</kanji> is <vocabulary>wheat flour</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Remember how 下品 is "crude" and "vulgar" - this is obviously the opposite. This is <vocabulary>elegant</vocabulary>.

This radical looks like a <radical>narwhal</radical>. See the tail at the bottom, and the majestic narwhal horn poking out at the top? It also looks like the katakana character ナ (na), so you can remember it that way too. Na-na-na-narwhal! Just be careful not to confuse this with the treasure radical (メ). The sideways line for that one is at more of a downward angle, like an "X." But the sideways line for narwhal is horizontal (ナ).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>front</kanji> <kanji>scene</kanji> is the <vocabulary>foreground</vocabulary>.

This word primarily refers to the visual foreground in art, photography, or theater. Unlike "foreground" in English, it’s not commonly used in a figurative sense to describe the most prominent aspect of situations.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just note that the とく goes to とっ.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
If you're involved in a <kanji>daring</kanji> <kanji>fight</kanji>, you're probably <vocabulary>fighting bravely</vocabulary>. You could get hurt, or worse, but you don't even care! Talk about fighting bravely… And good luck with that.

readingMnemonic: The reading is 言う and 訳 combined.
meaningMnemonic: You <kanji>say</kanji> a <kanji>reason</kanji> for your actions, but really it's just an <vocabulary>excuse</vocabulary>.

It's the drunkard from before, but this time she's leaning on some kind of horizontal surface. Knowing her, it's probably the counter of a <radical>bar</radical>. Hopefully she's not causing too much trouble for the bar staff with her drunken antics.

Crosses creep you out and this is way too many for you to keep walking so you decide to <kanji>run</kanji> as fast as you can to get past them.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>reef</kanji> made of <kanji>boulder</kanji>s is still a <vocabulary>reef</vocabulary>, but it's made of <vocabulary>sunken rocks</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

In Japan rice paddies are made up of square fields with irrigation lines going between them. See the four rice paddies with water flowing between and around them? That's why this radical is <radical>rice paddy</radical>.

readingMnemonic: You already have <kanji>color</kanji> on the mind because you know the meaning of this kanji, so think of something colorful about yourself. Imagine your <reading>ear</reading> (いろ) being a weird color... green, purple, red, whatever. Just make it really bright and standing out.

readingMnemonic: If someone seems <vocabulary>to be distressed</vocabulary> maybe someone they know is in a <reading>coma</reading> (こま). Not too many things are more distressing and troubling than that.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>distressed</kanji> and <kanji>troubled</kanji>. The verb versions of those are <vocabulary>to be distressed</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to be troubled</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: It has <kanji>simplicity</kanji> and is <kanji>easy</kanji>. Whatever it is, it is <vocabulary>simple</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>easy</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:

Every <vocabulary>eighth day</vocabulary> you have to buy <reading>yo</reading>gurt to fuel your <reading>ca</reading>r (ようか). Actually, verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!

readingMnemonic: The reading for 芝 is the one you learned with the kanji. The reading for 生 is one you haven't seen before (exception). It's ふ, and you can remember it by thinking how you were such a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ) for putting all that poison on it. Now it's dying, and now it's becoming less of a lawn.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Watch out for the shortened いち.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

The reading for 西 here is an exception. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

<vocabulary>Watermelon</vocabulary>s taste best after you <reading>swi</reading>ng (すい) them around. Whether you tie a rope to them or swing them on an actual swing, it mixes up the yummy watermelon insides and they end up tasting the best this way. readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

In terms of places where you want <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> your money, the last place on your list should be <reading>a zoo</reading> (あず). I mean seriously, you know the animals are just gonna munch up all your dolla bills.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to entrust</vocabulary>. 

You use 預ける when you leave something in someone else's care for a while, expecting to get it back. For example, you can use 預ける when you deposit money in a bank, leave your coat in a cloakroom, or even when you park your bicycle in a parking area. You can also use it when you leave your child with grandparents or leave your dog at a pet hotel.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>fluid</kanji> <kanji>crystal</kanji> is a <vocabulary>liquid crystal</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: My <kanji>behind</kanji> <kanji>regret</kanji> is the regret from before, which is all regret. So this means <vocabulary>regret</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>repentance</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 名 uses an alternate on'yomi reading here that you haven't learned yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Imagine you and your significant other are about to get hitched, and you're trying to decide your future <vocabulary>surname</vocabulary>. "Let's just combine 'me' and 'you' and go with <reading>Myou</reading> (みょう)," you say. Yes, from now on, you two will share the surname Myou.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>name</kanji> written in <kanji>letter</kanji>s is the <vocabulary>surname</vocabulary>. Back in the day your surname was the important name (it's your family name after all, and family was king back in the day). This is the name you'd write out in kanji... aka in letters. So, that's why this combination of kanji means "surname."

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just be sure to note the shortened しょく.
meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>eat</kanji>ing <kanji>container</kanji>s refer to <vocabulary>tableware</vocabulary>, including <vocabulary>eating utensils</vocabulary>, such as knives, forks, spoons, and chopsticks, as well as <vocabulary>serving utensils</vocabulary>, like plates, bowls, and saucers. Basically, it's stuff you use to eat your food.

readingMnemonic: As you <kanji>watch over</kanji> your friends and neighbors you see movement in the distance. Oh no, it's Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) and his army!
meaningMnemonic: Put your <radical>hand</radical> over your <radical>eye</radical> to <kanji>watch over</kanji> others.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Watch out for the rendaku.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>renew</kanji>ed and <kanji>revise</kanji>d <kanji>edition</kanji> of something is the <vocabulary>revised edition</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Ra, the Egyptian god asks you: "Can you do it? Are you <vocabulary>certain</vocabulary> you can build the pyramids?" 

"Yes I <reading>can ra</reading> (かなら). Yes I can," you reply.
meaningMnemonic: This word looks like a verb but it's not (sorry!). It's an adverb. The kanji itself means <kanji>certain</kanji> and the vocab version means all sorts of variations on that: <vocabulary>surely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>without exception</vocabulary> to name a few.

readingMnemonic: When you gather things, you go around and take things from their original location to put them together in your gathering spot. In Japanese, when you take something, you could say 取る, right? This word has the same reading: <reading>とる</reading>.
meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>gather</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to gather</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Careful because the 設 gets shortened to せっ.
meaningMnemonic:
What do you <kanji>establish</kanji> and <kanji>determine</kanji> in your every day life? A setting. When you make that into a verb, you have the word <vocabulary>to set</vocabulary>, as in setting the temperature of the AC, setting your password, or setting your computer to dark mode.

設定する is a little formal, but does get commonly used for device, system, and game settings. It's also often used in more official contexts, like for setting prices for products or establishing project goals.

readingMnemonic:
The first meaning is <vocabulary>one day</vocabulary>, and it has the same reading as the kanji you learned, so you should already know this reading.

The reading for ”first day," however, is a big old exception. It doesn’t take the on’yomi or kun’yomi readings, and has its own special (weird) readings. Here’s a mnemonic to help  you remember this one:

On the <vocabulary>first day</vocabulary> of a new relationship you just <reading>tweet a chee</reading>sy (ついたち) line at each other. You're so in love you can't speak normally, so you just use bird calls and cheesy lines to communicate.
meaningMnemonic: This word has two different meanings. <vocabulary>One day</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>first day</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this word, those meanings make a lot of sense.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Line up</kanji> everything in a <kanji>row</kanji>. When you do that, everything will be <vocabulary>side by side</vocabulary>.

並列 is a relatively formal word for things being arranged side by side in alignment. You'll most commonly see it used in a technical sense, like with <vocabulary>parallel</vocabulary> circuits in electronic stuff. But it's also used to describe the orderly side-by-side arrangements of other things, such as vehicles parked next to each other in a row or soldiers standing in ranks.

readingMnemonic: The reading is different from the other kun'yomi readings you've learned so far with this word. It is きたない. Think of it like you're saying "<reading>来た、な</reading>", as in "it came, huh?" What came? A really dirty looking monster, and it's coming for you.
meaningMnemonic: This is the adjective form of 汚, which is <kanji>dirty</kanji>. This word is the adjective <vocabulary>dirty</vocabulary>, but you can also use it to say things like <vocabulary>filthy</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>foul</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>unclean</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Towns <kanji>destitute</kanji> and <kanji>scarce</kanji> of food will end up in <vocabulary>poverty</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>destitution</vocabulary>.

meaningMnemonic: The <radical>rocket</radical> <radical>turkey</radical> has several points which will <kanji>detach</kanji> during takeoff.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Just watch out, as the 世 gets shortened from せい to せ! You can memorize this by remembering to be short and sweet with your flattery, don't make it too long and overcomplicated!
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>quit</kanji> your current <kanji>generation</kanji> to join an older one, you'll need to use all kinds of <vocabulary>flattery</vocabulary>. Older people love being flattered; so be nice and give them some <vocabulary>compliment</vocabulary>s.

readingMnemonic: Why do they <kanji>provide</kanji> and <kanji>equip</kanji> the cliff with flowers? It's all for the <reading>bee</reading>s (び).
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> put <radical>flowers</radical> on a <radical>cliff</radical>. That is their <radical>task</radical>. It is to <kanji>provide</kanji> and <kanji>equip</kanji> the cliff with flowers.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>range</kanji> is <kanji>outside</kanji> of the range, meaning you're <vocabulary>out of range</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
The おおさか reading for this word is made up of the kun'yomi for each kanji. You've learned the おお reading (like in 大きい), but you haven't seen the さか reading for 阪 yet. 

That said, doesn't 阪 look a lot like 坂, which also means "slope"? Turns out they share the さか reading as well, so if you remember the word 坂 you can apply that reading here. (In fact, 大阪 was sometimes written as 大坂 in the old days.) The easiest mnemonic is probably just to think of the city of  <vocabulary>Osaka</vocabulary> though… Just don't forget about the double おお.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>big</kanji> place called <kanji>Osaka</kanji>? This is the city of <vocabulary>Osaka</vocabulary>! Ever heard of it? It's a big city, and kind of the rival to Tokyo.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>image</kanji> <kanji>surface</kanji> is a <vocabulary>screen</vocabulary>. Just imagine your computer screen. There's an image on the surface, right? It just happens to move around all the time, like most images on screens these days.

readingMnemonic: Right <kanji>now</kanji> the <reading>con</reading>dors (こん) are in danger! Not next week, not next year, right now! Haven't you heard that deforestation and pollution are killing all of the condors?!

readingMnemonic: You have a <kanji>storehouse</kanji>. Inside is where you keep all your <reading>zo</reading>mbies (ぞう).
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>storehouse</radical> radical and the <kanji>storehouse</kanji> kanji meanings are the same. If you know the radical, you know the kanji!

readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji, though て goes to で.
meaningMnemonic: This is a weird one. Just think about the <kanji>sect</kanji> of <kanji>hand</kanji>s. They are always doing jazz hands and things like that, trying to be all <vocabulary>showy</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>flashy</vocabulary>. Ugh, what a dumb sect, you think.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Two</kanji> <kanji>bread loaf counter</kanji>s are counting <vocabulary>two loaves of bread</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!
meaningMnemonic: When a plant or an animal <kanji>die</kanji>s you have to <vocabulary>discard</vocabulary> it. You can't just keep it sitting around the house after <vocabulary>death</vocabulary>, that's weird.

readingMnemonic: "You have <kanji>rights</kanji>, so I won't shoot you like this turkey," says the voice of <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai, from above you in the tree.
meaningMnemonic: Under a <radical>tree</radical>, a broken <radical>arrow</radical> protrudes from a <radical>turkey</radical>. It was fighting for the <kanji>rights</kanji> of its fellow turkeys, and was mortally wounded in the process.

readingMnemonic: You know how when people are unconscious and their <kanji>breath</kanji> slows or comes to a stop, they use smelling salts to revive them? Well a smelly <reading>sock</reading> (そく) can work just as well. Socks get really stinky and their stench is powerful enough to revive someone who isn’t drawing breath.
meaningMnemonic: Imagining one’s <radical>self</radical> without a <radical>heart</radical> can make it hard to draw <kanji>breath</kanji>. Without a heart, you’d have no blood pumping and you would start to die. This would make it increasingly harder to draw breath and get oxygen to stay alive.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading, so you should be able to read this too!
meaningMnemonic:
If you go to (ごと) a <kanji>circle</kanji>, you need to go to it <vocabulary>in its entirety</vocabulary>. That means you have to circle around the <vocabulary>whole</vocabulary> thing. Otherwise, it isn't even a circle. It's like a line or a squiggle or something.

You often hear this word when talking about food – like when biting into a whole apple or accidentally swallowing a grape without chewing. But it's not just for food: you can also use it to talk about memorizing a whole book from beginning to end, for example.

readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>research</kanji> is on <reading>cu</reading>cumbers (きゅう)!
meaningMnemonic: You dig a <radical>hole</radical> <radical>nine</radical> times for your <kanji>research</kanji>. You should always do research with nine variables so you can compare them, and so there's an uneven number.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: This is seen on things like dictionaries. When you have an <kanji>English</kanji> and <kanji>Japanese</kanji> (style) dictionary, for example. You'll see it the other way around too, but this particular one is <vocabulary>English Japanese</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: How much can you hold in this <kanji>ladle</kanji>? Why, exactly <vocabulary>eighteen liters</vocabulary> of course! Eighteen is your favorite number, how convenient.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>road</radical>.

meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> <radical>squid</radical> tells all of its squid people to be <kanji>thrifty</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Deviate</kanji> from normal, everyday <kanji>product</kanji>s and buy lots of <vocabulary>gem</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>treasure</vocabulary>s! Especially if you're buying presents. Normal stuff just isn't going to cut it.

readingMnemonic: Both of these kanji take the on'yomi, but the first one has a slightly irregular reading, because it's based on the modern Chinese reading. To remember that it's a long らー, just think how excited you are about these ramen! <reading>Raaaaaa</reading>! Raaaamen! So exciting!
meaningMnemonic:
If you're going to <kanji>abduct</kanji> some <kanji>noodles</kanji>, make sure it's everybody's favorite noodles, <vocabulary>ramen</vocabulary>! The other meaning of the first kanji actually makes more sense here though, because you <kanji>pull</kanji> the dough to stretch it when you make <vocabulary>ramen noodles</vocabulary>. Choose whichever meaning helps you remember it best!

This word is mostly written in kana, usually as ラーメン, but sometimes らーめん. You'll see the kanji version pretty often on packaging and menus, though, so it's worth knowing! The word is also occasionally written as らー麺 or ラー麺.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When <kanji>orphan</kanji>s <kanji>stand</kanji>, they stand in <vocabulary>isolation</vocabulary> — <vocabulary>alone</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>friendless</vocabulary>. Orphans don't have any parents, so this world can be a pretty cruel place for them. It's really sad.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Erase</kanji> your need for normal <kanji>tea</kanji> by drinking <vocabulary>matcha</vocabulary>. It is far superior to all others and you'll never turn back once you've had a taste.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this is strange. It's the kun'yomi vocab reading, probably because the literal translation is "mother parent" and therefore consists of a couple words combined together into one concept. So, make sure you know the separate word readings of 母 and 親. If you do, you should be able to read this too.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>mother</kanji> <kanji>parent</kanji> is the <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You have to remember the はし portion. Think of yourself running. It's nice. As you run, though, you notice the ground changing into something weird and mushy. Everything is turning into <reading>hash</reading> (はし) browns. You start to get sucked in, and soon you can't run anymore. Smell the hash browns and taste them too. What a terrible run this was.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>run</kanji> so now you know the verb version of that is <vocabulary>to run</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: "Oh, did he <vocabulary>go</vocabulary> again?" When <reading>こう</reading>いち is not around, that's what people often say because he goes to the <reading>gyo</reading>za (ぎょう) restaurant almost every day. こういち just loves gyoza so much, you always know where he is when he is not home.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>go</radical> radical and the <kanji>go</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn this reading for 元 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Who's always there on the dawn of <vocabulary>New Year's Day</vocabulary> welcoming the new sun? <reading>Gan</reading>dhi (がん). He sits on the edge of the earth and makes sure the sun feels welcome. What a nice guy.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>origin</kanji> of <kanji>dawn</kanji> can be found on <vocabulary>New Year's Day</vocabulary>. That's when the new sun is born and rises above the earth for a whole year until it dies. And that's the origin of dawn, children. Don't let your teachers tell you otherwise.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

I have a lot of <vocabulary>anger</vocabulary> because <reading>I ca</reading>rry (いか) all of my own things (books, luggage, drinks) and no one will ever carry them for me. Plus, the more things I carry, the more anger I carry inside. Ahh!
meaningMnemonic: This word looks a lot like 怒る, doesn't it? But this word isn't a verb, so you can think of it as referring to <vocabulary>anger</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wrath</vocabulary> itself.

readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You smell someone's <reading>icky</reading> (いき) <vocabulary>breath</vocabulary>. It's gross. Your skin crawls and your eyes roll back in your head from the icky, icky smell. You might die.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: The most <kanji>gold</kanji> in the land belongs to the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England. In fact, you've never actually met someone with gold, it all goes straight to the King whenever someone finds some. You just have a few pennies to work with.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>gold</radical> radical and the <kanji>gold</kanji> kanji are the same!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>director</kanji> who is <kanji>above</kanji> you is your <vocabulary>boss</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>superior</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi, which is usually the case when there's hiragana in the middle. You learned the reading for 買い when you learned the kanji, as well as the word 買う, and you learned this reading of 物 in the word 物!
meaningMnemonic: You've hopefully seen 買う by now and know it means "to buy." So, 買い is going to be similar to that. Add that to <kanji>thing</kanji> and you have a "buying things" sort of word. What does "buying things" describe? It describes <vocabulary>shopping</vocabulary>.

建前 is very important in Japan. For example, you might find yourself invited to an acquaintance's home out of courtesy, with the expectation that you’ll decline (also out of courtesy!). A host of a party may say "just bring yourself," but guests know this could be 建前, and considering their own 建前, they bring a small gift anyways.  People can also be reluctant to say "no" to things, like drinks with coworkers when they really want to go home, and may not to show it when they find situations inconvenient or unpleasant. So you might need some guesswork to peek behind the 建前 that people build up in front of themselves!

Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. 間 has two common kun'yomi readings, あいだ and ま. You haven't learned these readings yet, so here's an explanation of each reading and mnemonics to help you remember them:

間 is usually read as あいだ for a longer interval of time or general space between things. It's read as ま for a short burst of time or when defining a specific area, like a 茶の間 (the older name for a Japanese living room).

You can remember this because time feels longer in <reading>Ida</reading>ho (あいだ). Any interval of time you spend there feels so long, because Idaho life moves so slowly. As soon as you cross the border and enter a new state, you call your <reading>ma</reading> (ま) to tell her you're finally out of that slooooow state, and the intervals of time feel shorter.
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Hanging off the cliff, the child cries out to the sun to save them from this cruel fate. You're able <vocabulary>to relax</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to feel at home</vocabulary> because nothing really gets to you.

meaningMnemonic:

This word is generally used in the names of gardens, like エデンの園 and 桜の園. It's also used in phrases like 学びの園, which means "school" and carries the connotation of being a haven for learning.

meaningMnemonic: This is the words 背 and 高い put together to make one adjective. When your height is tall it means you are a <vocabulary>tall</vocabulary> person. This word is only used for tall people though, not anything else that's tall like a building or a tree.

<kanji>Ten thousand</kanji> <kanji>year</kanji>s! That's a lot of time. This is the word for the turned-English Japanese phrase, <vocabulary>banzai</vocabulary>!

万歳 is a cheerful word used to shout "<vocabulary>hooray</vocabulary>!" when celebrating something good. Because it's usually said with both arms raised, the action of <vocabulary>raising one's arms</vocabulary> can also be referred to as 万歳. This is often used when talking to children, like when telling them to raise their arms to take off a shirt.

And since raising your hands can also mean "<vocabulary>I give up</vocabulary>" in Japan, 万歳 can sometimes mean that as well. So basically, it's either "Yay, we did it!" or "That's it, I'm done." It really covers all your bases!

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned the on'yomi for 狼 (wolf) yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember that, as well as which on'yomi to use for 人:

There's a <vocabulary>werewolf</vocabulary> in front of you wearing  <reading>jean</reading>s and eating <reading>roe</reading> (じんろう). This is typical behavior for werewolves, as I'm sure you know.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji> <kanji>wolf </kanji> is a <vocabulary>werewolf</vocabulary>. This word is less common than 狼男, but it's used more and more thanks to the card game of the same name!

readingMnemonic:
You're running out of steam and you're afraid you might not be able to <kanji>detain</kanji> all of these guys when <reading>Ryu</reading> (りゅう) from Street Fighter appears. He hates swords, and will only use fists because it's the honorable way to fight, so he starts helping you detain them!

He's also found a <reading>loo</reading>phole (る) in the system and you don't have to be super gentle with these guys either. So detain them as forcefully as you want. It is your rice paddy they're in, after all.
meaningMnemonic: A group of <radical>private</radical> <radical>sword</radical> guys are in your <radical>rice paddy</radical>. You must <kanji>detain</kanji> them at once! Private sword guys are people who work for private companies and use their swords on people. They're basically paid assassins. And you're going to detain them!

readingMnemonic: The reading is shared with 載る, so as long as you remember that you can remember this.
meaningMnemonic:
Remember how 載る is "to be placed on"? This one is <vocabulary>to place on something</vocabulary>, like a mug on a table. 載せる is transitive, and you know this because you do it your<reading>sel</reading>f (せる). Like 載る, 載せる also often refers to putting something in a written document or publication, so it can mean <vocabulary>to put on record</vocabulary>.

Note that 載せる is never used to refer to putting clothing or accessories on. That's 着る or 着ける respectively, which you've learned already.

readingMnemonic: You <kanji>dig</kanji> until you finally hit something. It's a bunch of buried old <reading>coots</reading> (くつ). They're in an underground room for old coots. One yells up at you, "Whatcha doing to our roof, ya whipper snapper?! Stop digging in our lawn!"

The fingers on the flag point downward, just by the exit, as if to say "dig here!" There must be something under here. That's what you think to yourself as you start to dig with your fingers.

meaningMnemonic: You know the word 皿 (plate) and the word 洗う (to wash), right? You can probably guess dish washing is happening here, but this is a noun, so it's the idea of <vocabulary>dishwashing</vocabulary>, AKA <vocabulary>doing dishes</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>washing dishes</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: While using the jackhammer on the <kanji>ballot</kanji>, the helicopter pilot keeps yelling “<reading>Heyo</reading> (ひょう), don't mess up! Heyo! Watch out, don't let me see!” as he flies the helicopter all over the place.
meaningMnemonic: You have to fly in a <radical>helicopter</radical> and use a <radical>jackhammer</radical> to punch your <kanji>ballot</kanji>. The helicopter gets you far away from prying eyes, and the jackhammer makes you really try for whoever you're voting for on that thing. It's foolproof!
