meaningMnemonic: You plant your <radical>flowers</radical> in the light of the <radical>sun</radical> in the shape of a <radical>cross</radical>, but it's too hot—the sun is too strong—and you end up with <kanji>grass</kanji>. Flowers can't grow in these conditions.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>name</kanji> <kanji>part of speech</kanji> is when you are naming something. What part of speech has names in it? That would be the <vocabulary>noun</vocabulary>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>director</radical>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you want <vocabulary>to get thin</vocabulary>, just join the <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (や). They run their players around those four bases so much they all get thin quicker than you can throw a ball.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>thin</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to get thin</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the reading you learned for the kanji 爪 and the word for the reading 切る.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>cut</kanji> your <kanji>claw</kanji> you use a <vocabulary>nail clipper</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for 何 and the on'yomi reading for 月. You learned those readings with the kanji, but since 何 and 月 both have two readings, here's a mnemonic to help you out: What month will you choose to get naan guts (なんがつ) in? You've gotta pick a month to gorge yourself on naan until your guts are absolutely stuffed with it. But which month will you choose? Think about it! Note: 何月 isn't a specific month name, but as a question word, it is asking for a specific month on the calendar — which is why がつ gets used here.
meaningMnemonic: You have <kanji>what</kanji> <kanji>month</kanji> - as in: <vocabulary>what month</vocabulary> is it? It's １０月, you fool. Get a job, hippy.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: If you see the kanji <kanji>restaurant</kanji> attached to a place name, there's a good chance that it's a <vocabulary>restaurant</vocabulary>, especially a <vocabulary>traditional Japanese restaurant</vocabulary>. It also crops up on the end of other places where you can rest, like <vocabulary>inn</vocabulary>s, those traditional <vocabulary>pavilion</vocabulary>s you see in Japanese parks and temple grounds, and <vocabulary>tea house</vocabulary>s.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Counting days, however, is an exception (at least up to ten). You need to use the kun'yomi readings to read this word. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 四, so that's fine (the ん gets turned into a small っ, though). Think of it this way:

On the <vocabulary>fourth day</vocabulary> of being lost in the wilderness, you start yelling "<reading>Yo</reading>, <reading>ca</reading>r (よっか)!" out of desperation, never getting an answer. You keep marching on, occasionally yelling "Yo, car!", but no car ever comes to help you.
meaningMnemonic: <vocabulary>Fourth day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>day four</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this combination of kanji, the meaning of the word makes a lot of sense!

readingMnemonic:
You learned this reading with the kanji, how nice for you!

However, you might notice that in addition to うめる, there's another reading too: うずめる. うめる is used for the act of burying something or filling in a hole, while うずめる is used when describing the covering or concealment of something, or when burying one's face in something (like a fluffy cat!)
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bury</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to bury</vocabulary> as well.

埋める can also mean <vocabulary>to fill</vocabulary>, and can refer to filling a hole, vacancy, or gap. Note that this word can be used to refer to filling in figurative holes and gaps too, like a hole in one’s finances!

readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them already, so you should be able to read this on your own. Just remember that there is rendaku on こと and it becomes ごと.
meaningMnemonic: Learner, if you <kanji>see</kanji> a <kanji>thing</kanji>, then it must be <vocabulary>splendid</vocabulary>. You saw it, after all, so of course it's <vocabulary>magnificent</vocabulary>. You only see the <vocabulary>beautiful</vocabulary> things in this world. And that's an <vocabulary>admirable</vocabulary> quality.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You want <vocabulary>to compose</vocabulary> a poem but all you have for inspiration is what's in your pocket. You reach in and find a <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ). Ah yes, this will do. So you compose a poem about your yo-yo:

One string to rule them all,
One string to find them,
One string to- hey wait a minute...
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>compose</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to compose</vocabulary>.

テレビ comes from the English word <vocabulary>television</vocabulary>. It’s been shortened, which is really common with loanwords in Japanese. The "vi" sound becomes ビ, too.

テレビ is sometimes written as "TV", but even then it’s usually pronounced テレビ.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with this kanji, but here's a reminder of the mnemonic just in case: 

You have to remember the おも part to read this word. To do this, though, you'll have <vocabulary>to think</vocabulary> about that guy... hmm... what was his name? He's on The Simpsons... he's the bartender? I think? <reading>Oh! Moe</reading> (おも) is his name! Thank you. Now I remember.

If you don't know Moe from the Simpsons use a different Moe, perhaps the one from the Three Stooges? You should be able to come up with one.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>think</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to think</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. How strange! Or not.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is more the "strange" meaning though, not the "change" one. As in, you 変な猫！

readingMnemonic: Is this <kanji>convex</kanji>? It's <reading>totes</reading> (とつ) convex!
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>convex</radical> radical and the <kanji>convex</kanji> kanji are the same, so hopefully you now just know them both.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this is the stem form of both verbs, so 締め (しめ) and 切り (きり), put together!
meaningMnemonic:
Things 締める (tighten), and eventually 切る (cut off), meaning you’ve reached the <vocabulary>deadline</vocabulary>! You can associate this with the feeling of your chest tightening once you approach the <vocabulary>due date</vocabulary> for something.

Note that you'll often encounter this written with okurigana like 締め切り as well. You might even see it with a simplified version of the 締 kanji written 〆切, which is relatively common in handwriting!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: It's <kanji>certain</kanji> that you <kanji>need</kanji> it. This thing is <vocabulary>necessary</vocabulary>. It is <vocabulary>needed</vocabulary>.
This looks like something you'd put on a kettle or a pot, right? It even has a little handle to make sure you don't burn yourself. This is some kind of <radical>lid</radical>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: An <kanji>aviation</kanji> (航空) <kanji>ticket</kanji> is the kind of ticket you need to fly on an airplane. That's an <vocabulary>airplane ticket</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ぱ at the end is the only tricky part here since that isn't a common reading (or the one you learned before) for the kanji. Just think of your ol' <reading>Pa</reading> (ぱ), who is the biggest half-asser you know.
meaningMnemonic: Take the <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>route</kanji>, <kanji>half</kanji> to the <kanji>edge</kanji>. You don't do anything the full way. Just to the middle. Just to the half. Not to the edge. This was really <vocabulary>half finished</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>half assed</vocabulary> of you.

readingMnemonic: To make sure that no one removes your <kanji>flag</kanji>, you lock it to one of the lifeguard posts and you throw away the <reading>key</reading> (き). Since no one will have the key to unlock the flag, no one will be able to remove it.
meaningMnemonic: Traveling in the <radical>direction</radical> of the ocean, you take a <radical>gun</radical> and shoot a <radical>crab</radical>, then stick a <kanji>flag</kanji> in the beach and claim it as your own. The crab was the only thing standing in the way of you conquering the area. Now that the flag is in the ground, no one can dispute who it belongs to.

readingMnemonic: For example, you're bound <vocabulary>to get tired</vocabulary> if you try to lift <reading>two ca</reading>rs (つか), right? So think about that as you learn this word's reading.
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>tired</kanji>, so the verb version means <vocabulary>to get tired</vocabulary>. 

疲れる refers to a physical or mental kind of tiredness, like you just worked out or studied a ton, but isn't used to describe sleepiness.

readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same.

readingMnemonic: When you look at the <kanji>scroll</kanji> you realize... you look just like Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん)! You excitedly fist pump and start showing everyone how cool you are.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>gladiator</radical> only sees himself (<radical>oneself</radical>) on those big <kanji>scroll</kanji>s they advertise the fights with. Gladiators don't get mirrors and there are no cameras or videos yet. The scroll drawings are all they get of themselves.

readingMnemonic: This word uses on'yomi reading, which you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: The name of the city (シアトル／しあとる) with a <kanji>市</kanji> attached to it means it is "the city of ____." You can do this with any city (try it out on your hometown!). So this word means <vocabulary>Seattle</vocabulary>, or more specifically <vocabulary>City of Seattle</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>public building</kanji> where you <kanji>welcome</kanji> <kanji>VIP</kanji> guests is a <vocabulary>reception hall</vocabulary>. Or a <vocabulary>guest house</vocabulary> if they're staying the night.

readingMnemonic: The reading is a combination of on'yomi for the first two and kun'yomi for the last one. That being said, all of the readings for all of the kanji are the readings you've learned already, so you should be able to read this word too. Just watch out because ひ is rendaku'd into び.
meaningMnemonic:
You should <kanji>write down</kanji> all your <kanji>thoughts</kanji> on this <kanji>day</kanji>, because it's not just any day — it's an <vocabulary>anniversary</vocabulary>!

Wondering how 記念日 differs from 周年? 周年 is usually for a numbered anniversary, like 十周年 (10th anniversary), whereas 記念日 refers to the specific date on which a memorable event took place in the past.

readingMnemonic: Each <kanji>state</kanji> has its own <reading>shoe</reading> (しゅう) to represent it. The bottom of each shoe is the shape of the state, so when you step it leaves a state-shaped imprint in the ground.
meaningMnemonic: Think about Japan. Japan is a country made up of islands. They're basically three <radical>drop</radical> <radical>drop</radical> <radical>drop</radical>s in the large <radical>river</radical> that is the Pacific Ocean. These are Japan's <kanji>states</kanji> or <kanji>province</kanji>s.

readingMnemonic:
You have to remember the う part of this word to read it. To remember that, let's use a mnemonic: 

Something is about to be born, and when you lean in for a closer look… it’s an <reading>u</reading>ni (う). Yes, a sea urchin. You weren’t expecting that. Close your eyes and imagine what the process of an uni being born might look like, to help you remember this reading.
meaningMnemonic: Since this is a kanji with hiragana attached that ends with an う sound, you know that this word is a verb. What's the ultimate verb version of the kanji 生? That would be <vocabulary>to be born</vocabulary>, the very beginning of <kanji>life</kanji> as we know it!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji, and you've learned both. Just remember that 楽 uses its secondary reading がく when it's in music-related words!
meaningMnemonic: Remember how 楽 was used in 音楽 (music)? Well this is that 楽 again. So this is <kanji>string</kanji> <kanji>music</kanji>, which of course means <vocabulary>string music</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>profit</kanji> from your <kanji>convenience</kanji>, that means you have something very <vocabulary>convenient</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>handy</vocabulary>. Remember, you can profit in other ways besides money. This convenience could be giving you a profit in happiness or extra time as well. All these things are very handy to have.

readingMnemonic: As you watch your mama <kanji>pass through</kanji> the house, she yells, "YOU HAVE TO DO THIS TASK <reading>TOO</reading> (つう)!" Too?! Oh no, now you have to do it too. Hurry up!
meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>scooter</radical> with your <radical>mama</radical> carrying a <radical>task</radical> she needs to get done. You see her <kanji>pass through</kanji>, hurrying by to get that task done.

readingMnemonic: To make sure people listen to your <kanji>warn</kanji>ing, you threaten to take away their <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい). People will do anything for cake, so when you bring it up, they actually take your attempts to warn them about winter seriously.
meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>poem</radical> about <radical>winter</radical> that you <radical>say</radical> to <kanji>warn</kanji> people against going outside. It's cold and dangerous in winter! You <kanji>admonish</kanji> anyone and everyone you see going out there with your scary winter poem.

readingMnemonic:
The reading for this word is pretty strange. It changes depending on the type of verb form you use (it's a pesky exception verb). To remember the reading of this word, here's a mnemonic: 

"I want you <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary> to the <reading>coo</reading>l (く) side, Luke," says Darth Vader.
"What?" replies Luke.

Just replace this line into the famous line from Star Wars. Say it out loud. Do the Vader voice. It'll help you to remember.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>come</kanji> so you know this word means <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The first <kanji>edition</kanji> you create is a fan fiction all about the adventures of <reading>Han</reading> (はん) Solo. You hated how short and one-sided his story in Star Wars seemed to be, and trying to keep track of it all was really hard. But not anymore!
meaningMnemonic: If you're a <radical>one-sided</radical> paper <radical>anti</radical> (someone against one-sided paper), then you should bind all those one-sided papers into an <kanji>edition</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: Now it's summertime! What do you do during the <kanji>summer</kanji>? You just sit around with your favorite string tying <reading>knots</reading> (なつ) in it over and over again.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leaf</radical> shaped like an <radical>eye</radical> only grows in <radical>winter</radical>. Every other leaf, however, will do the opposite, which is to grow in the <kanji>summer</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you're <kanji>overcome</kanji> with <kanji>bright</kanji>ness, you'll be able to see all the little fine <vocabulary>detailed</vocabulary> things.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is pretty weird. It's different than the 嫌い word you will see in this level too. It is いや, so when you think of something you dislike, just think "<reading>iyah</reading> (いや), I dislike it." Also, think about that <vocabulary>eww</vocabulary> feeling it gives you when you think of the thing you dislike most.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. The vocab has the added meanings of <vocabulary>eww</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>gross</vocabulary>, and even <vocabulary>reluctant</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is 草 and 刈 put together into one. The か reading for 刈り comes from the kanji's reading.
meaningMnemonic: Let's take the <kanji>grass</kanji> and <kanji>prune</kanji> it. This is called <vocabulary>mowing</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Imagine a numerical <vocabulary>value</vocabulary> written on <reading>a tie</reading> (あたい). Now imagine that it's the <vocabulary>price</vocabulary> of a <reading>ne</reading>igh (ね) from your favorite horse. It's a pretty high price, but you'll do anything to hear that horse neigh.

Generally, あたい refers to a numerical value in math, while ね is a formal word for "price."
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>value</kanji> is a <vocabulary>value</vocabulary>, but only in the mathematical sense.

Depending on the reading, this can also mean <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Actually, before she can <kanji>begin</kanji>, she has to shear the <reading>shee</reading>p (し) over there. The machine is going to turn wool into yarn, but you can't just start that process by shoving the sheep in there. You have to keep the little sheep safe!
meaningMnemonic: If you give a <radical>woman</radical> a <radical>machine</radical> she'll <kanji>begin</kanji> learning how to use it right away. She'll also get it to <kanji>start</kanji> before anyone else could. Women are really good at starting up new machines!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>wind</radical>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>take along</kanji> some things that are <kanji>related</kanji>, you'll be able to understand their <vocabulary>relation</vocabulary> better.

readingMnemonic: You <kanji>scream</kanji> and scream and scream until a door bursts open. It's Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) and he looks mad. Apparently your screaming is bothering him and now he's gonna give you a real reason to scream.
meaningMnemonic: What would your <radical>mouth</radical> do if you got caught in a <radical>prison</radical> for <radical>legs</radical>? It'd probably get real <radical>big</radical> — in other words, it would <kanji>scream</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: When you need a moon <vocabulary>to be leaned</vocabulary>, your best option is to <reading>cut a moo</reading>n (かたむ) in half. It's impossible for a full moon <vocabulary>to be tilted</vocabulary>, but a split moon can lean one way or the other.
meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>lean</kanji>, and the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to be leaned</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be tilted</vocabulary>. You aren't doing the leaning or the tilting, though, you're just watching, which is why you say "cool" (く) when you see it, because it's already done.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already with the kanji, so you should be all set. Lucky you!
meaningMnemonic: This is a strange word, so you'll have to bear with me. You know that 知 means <kanji>know</kanji>. But in the case of this word, what do you know? Look at the second half. らせ sounds a bit like "race." So, you know about a "race." How do you know about this race? You got a <vocabulary>notice</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>notification</vocabulary> about it.

readingMnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi of 元 and then it's just kana, so you should know how to read this!
meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>origin</kanji> partner is a partner you had originally, but don't have anymore. In other words, this is your <vocabulary>ex-partner</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>former partner</vocabulary>.

Like in English, this word is fairly formal, and it covers any kind of ex-partner, including business and romantic partners.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, but it shares a reading (and some similarities in meaning) with 答える, so just try to think of that vocab in relation to this one!
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>respond</kanji>, and this is also <vocabulary>to respond to</vocabulary>, but often in the sense of trying <vocabulary>to meet</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to live up to</vocabulary> some expectation, need, or other feelings.

Check out our common word combinations and context sentences for some example usages of this!

This is the <radical>tongue</radical> radical. See that sturdy slide holding a thousand people above a mouth? An open mouth can't support that much weight, but a strong tongue can — it's the muscle of the mouth, after all.

Alternatively, you can think of this as something sticking out of a mouth with thousands of tiny taste buds on it. It's your tongue!

readingMnemonic: So now you're <kanji>bored</kanji> and stuck at <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう). You aren't hungry. There's nothing on TV. And you don't want to have to leave your home to do something, even though that would probably solve your boredom problem.
meaningMnemonic: You <radical>eat</radical> and then <radical>wrap</radical> yourself into a ball because you're <kanji>bored</kanji>. You're also <kanji>sated</kanji>, because you ate just the right amount, but now you have nothing to do and it's soooo booooring.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Go ahead and <kanji>put</kanji> a <kanji>rank</kanji> on something. This one is rank #1, so its <vocabulary>position</vocabulary> is up higher. Then you put a rank #67 on something. That one's position is lower.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>life</kanji> <kanji>horizon</kanji> is your life, which you're looking out over, all the way to the very end. This is <vocabulary>one's lifetime</vocabulary>, though it could also refer to <vocabulary>one's career</vocabulary>. Basically, at the end of it something dies.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 出口 is an exception to this rule, however, and uses its kun'yomi readings. There's no particular reason why this is, but oftentimes a "body part" word (like mouth) changes a word to use kun'yomi readings instead of on'yomi ones. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 口 (くち) from learning the vocab, but to remember the reading for 出 you can think the following:

If I exit out this mouth, I'll end up in the ocean (you were swallowed by a whale) and I will surely end up <reading>dea</reading>d (で).

Also keep in mind that because of rendaku, くち becomes ぐち.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>mouth</kanji> you <kanji>exit</kanji> out of is just a doorway (I hope), but an easier way to describe this word or concept is to call it an <vocabulary>exit</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>go</kanji> to <kanji>move</kanji> you're actually making an <vocabulary>action</vocabulary>. This word can also mean <vocabulary>behavior</vocabulary>, since your actions are what make up your behavior.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>seal</kanji> that's <kanji>model</kanji>ed after you is a useful <vocabulary>seal</vocabulary> indeed — it's your very own <vocabulary>personal seal</vocabulary>!

印鑑 is a small stamp with your name carved into it. In Japan, people use it on official documents instead of signing their name. It's like your legally recognized "signature stamp," and it's something most adults in Japan need to have.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
An <kanji>electricity</kanji> <kanji>lamp</kanji> is exactly what it sounds like: an <vocabulary>electric light</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>electric lamp</vocabulary>.

電灯 is a slightly technical word that broadly refers to electrical lighting. It can include many kinds of lighting devices, such as light bulbs, fluorescent lamps, streetlights, and flashlights, but it's most commonly used for a fixed light that illuminates a room or street.

readingMnemonic: The readings here are the vocab kun'yomi readings. You have ひ for 日 and や for 焼け (which you learned with the vocab). Combine it with some sunscreen and hopefully you'll prevent the <vocabulary>sunburn</vocabulary>.
meaningMnemonic: When the <kanji>sun</kanji> <kanji>burn</kanji>s something, and that something is you, it's giving you <vocabulary>sunburn</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: When people have just <vocabulary>a few</vocabulary> of something, <reading>wars</reading> (わず) tend to break out. So many wars have started because there was only <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> of something and people began to fight over it.
meaningMnemonic:
When something is <kanji>slight</kanji>, that means you only have <vocabulary>a few</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> of that thing.

僅か is a relatively formal word that indicates a small amount. You'll hear it when someone wants to emphasize how little something is, like 僅かな差 (a little gap) or 僅か10分 (<vocabulary>just</vocabulary> ten minutes). Note this word is often written in kana, as わずか, unless the writing style is very formal.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You like to use your <vocabulary>hand drum</vocabulary> when <reading>two du</reading>des <reading>mee</reading>t (つづみ). You drum and tap it as they high five and it makes them super uncomfortable which makes you super happy. That's why you love your hand drum so much.
meaningMnemonic: What do you hit to make a sick <kanji>beat</kanji>? A cool little <vocabulary>hand drum</vocabulary>.

This radical is made up of horns and older brother. But those aren't really horns, they're a part of your older brother's new <radical>guard</radical> uniform. He's a guard now, of a bank or a museum. You don't know which, but you know he stands around a lot in his uniform now.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hang</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to hang something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hang up something</vocabulary> (as in to hang it up by a hook).

You can remember this because you must <reading>care</reading> (ける) about the way you hang something up. Without care, it won't stay hanging for long.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>Japanese style</kanji> <kanji>room</kanji> tends to be pretty small. This mainly refers to the kind of room that's covered in tatami mats, though. If you're looking for places to stay in Japan, a 和室 will be something like that. You'll pull the futon out of the closet and sleep on the floor. So comfy, these <vocabulary>Japanese style room</vocabulary>s!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>giant</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is <vocabulary>a giant</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>shining</kanji> <kanji>peace</kanji> time was a time known as the <vocabulary>Showa Era</vocabulary>. This can also refer to the <vocabulary>Showa Emperor</vocabulary> or just <vocabulary>Showa</vocabulary> itself. Everything Showa is here.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>line up</radical>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: Despite looking like an adjective this is a noun. It means the same thing as the kanji: <vocabulary>curse</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: All of his <kanji>affair</kanji>s are taken care of by <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai, who he hired as his underling.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>cow</radical> tribe is too important to deal with small <kanji>matter</kanji>s and trivial <kanji>affair</kanji>s.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this kanji is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. That in itself isn't too <vocabulary>rare</vocabulary>, wouldn't you say?
meaningMnemonic:
Something <kanji>rare</kanji> is often <vocabulary>unusual</vocabulary>. This word could also mean <vocabulary>rare</vocabulary> (of course) and <vocabulary>peculiar</vocabulary> depending on the context.

These days, media often uses this word to describe the way something is unusual, quirky, and funny.

readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 緩む, so you can use that!
meaningMnemonic: 緩む is "to loosen," but has to do with loosening on its own. This word is when you loosen or relax something, meaning <vocabulary>to loosen</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to relax</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You visit the <vocabulary>sea</vocabulary>. Strangely, it asks you who is visiting. You're so full of yourself (even in front of the sea/ocean) that you reply: "<reading>um, me</reading>?" (うみ). Imagine yourself feeling this full of yourself.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: If you're going to get stabbed, don't get stabbed <reading>two</reading> (つ) times. You can remember that this is the "two time stab" stab because it has a hole that's big. The hole is big because you got stabbed twice.
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stab</kanji> so the verb vocab version must also be <vocabulary>to stab</vocabulary>.

Wondering how it's different from 刺す? 突く refers to the act of pushing or pressing something with a tip of an object, often done forcefully and swiftly. So when you use 突く as in "to stab," your focus is on the forcefulness of the action. On the other hand, 刺す focuses more on the actual act of piercing into something or someone with a sharp thing. 

This is why 突く can be be translated many ways, like <vocabulary>to poke</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to jab</vocabulary>, and many more.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: What do you call a <kanji>husband</kanji> and his <kanji>lady</kanji>? <vocabulary>Husband and wife</vocabulary>! They're a <vocabulary>married couple</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: It's <vocabulary>regrettable</vocabulary> if you're not <reading>coo</reading>l, <reading>yah</reading> (くや)? Yah, that would be pretty <vocabulary>vexing</vocabulary>.
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>regret</kanji> and this is <vocabulary>regrettable</vocabulary>. And something regrettable is likely to be <vocabulary>frustrating</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>vexing</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>disappointing</vocabulary>.

悔しい generally expresses a feeling of frustration, regret, or vexation, often due to a sense of failure or missed opportunity. It conveys a strong emotional response to a situation where one feels disappointed or bitter about not achieving something they desired, especially when they were close to success or when the outcome feels unfair.

readingMnemonic:
You know how to read the 揚げ part, but this uses the kun'yomi reading for 唐, which is new. You'll likely be able to remember this reading by associating fried chicken with Japanese karaage, but in case you're not familiar with it, here's a mnemonic to help you:

To make this kind of <vocabulary>fried chicken</vocabulary>, you have to first give it one strong <reading>から</reading>て chop. If you fry it up without that からて chop, it just comes out terrible no matter what you do. So just remember that next time you make it for me, kay?
meaningMnemonic:
You've got a combination of <kanji>China</kanji> and 揚げ, meaning "fried." That makes this Chinese-style <vocabulary>Fried Chicken</vocabulary>, or as you'll probably also know it, <vocabulary>karaage</vocabulary>.

While 唐揚げ most often refers to fried chicken, it can technically also refer to other deep fried meats, fish, or vegetables. As it's the most common meaning, remembering this as "fried chicken" will be just fine, though.

readingMnemonic: Since you already know the vocab word 今 (read いま), you should be able to read this word as well.
meaningMnemonic: You'll have to learn this word in two parts. You already know the meaning of 今 because of the kanji, which means "now." The すぐ part, however, is a new word, meaning "soon." すぐ and "soon" even start with a similar sound, so maybe that can help you remember this! If you put 今 and すぐ together, you get "now soon." Put in better English, that's <vocabulary>at once</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>right now</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Describe</kanji> someone's <kanji>merit</kanji> at a ceremony for the <vocabulary>conferring of decorations</vocabulary>. That's when medals are given out to people who deserve them. Usually in the military or something.

readingMnemonic: The readings are 猿 plus 真似 put together.
meaningMnemonic:
If 真似 is <kanji>imitation</kanji> and if a <kanji>monkey</kanji> is doing said imitation, that's summed up by the saying: <vocabulary>monkey see monkey do</vocabulary>.

This refers to when someone does a <vocabulary>mindless imitation</vocabulary> of others without any real thought, so is often used when criticizing people.

readingMnemonic: You may think it's just his <kanji>robust</kanji> body, but it's actually the samurai's robust <reading>sou</reading>l (そう) that keeps him fighting through the cold and the icicles.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>samurai</radical> who can fight with <radical>icicle</radical>s on him is more <kanji>robust</kanji> than regular samurai. Can you imagine how robust you'd have to be to fight in weather cold enough to form icicles on your body?

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
If you're on a <kanji>route</kanji>, right in the <kanji>middle</kanji>, you're <vocabulary>on the way</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>en route</vocabulary>.

途中 can also be used figuratively to say you're <vocabulary>in the middle of</vocabulary> doing something or something is <vocabulary>half done</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Watch out for the rendaku.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>neighbor</kanji> <kanji>country</kanji> is a <vocabulary>neighboring country</vocabulary>. For us, our 隣国 in America are those sneaky Canadians... always waiting to strike, I can tell...

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own — just watch out for ふ turning into ぷ due to rendaku here.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>pregnant</kanji> <kanji>lady</kanji> is a <vocabulary>pregnant woman</vocabulary>. How simple is that!

妊婦 is a relatively formal term used to refer to a woman who is pregnant. In casual situations it's common to add さん and say 妊婦さん, to make it sound friendlier.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Unlike the 警視庁, who look at things, this is just the <kanji>police officer</kanji> (警察) <kanji>agency</kanji>. Just the general police agency of the whole country, making them part of the <vocabulary>National Police Agency</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Renew</kanji> and make something <kanji>correct</kanji>. When you do this, you are doing a <vocabulary>revision</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>amendment</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>alteration</vocabulary>. Ah, much better now.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is the polite and humble form of <vocabulary>father</vocabulary>. You use this when you're talking about your own <vocabulary>dad</vocabulary> to other people in formal settings, especially if you aren't very close to them.

readingMnemonic: You know the word 先ず (まず)? It means something along the lines of "first of all." So, if you're <vocabulary>poor</vocabulary>, <reading>first of all</reading> (まず), you're going to want to get some help. Second of all, learn how to play the guitar and make funny jokes.
meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>poor</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>poor</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: You've only met one other person with the same mark on their <kanji>leg</kanji> and it was <reading>Kyaku</reading> (きゃく) the customer. Kyaku visits many places all over the world, so it only makes sense that they've also been off-world too.
meaningMnemonic: If you've been to the <radical>moon</radical> in the <radical>past</radical>, you had to get the special <radical>stamp</radical> on your <kanji>leg</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: If you get moist or moistened, then <reading>you're all</reading> (うるお) wet. It's just how it is.
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>watered</kanji>. When something is watered it becomes moist, right? That's why this verb is <vocabulary>to be moist</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be moistened</vocabulary>.

潤う refers to things being well-moisturized, like skin or eyes. Think of them as being enriched with moisture. That's why the meaning also extends to financial prosperity — moisture enriches the body, and financial gain enriches your life or business. So this word also means <vocabulary>to be prosperous</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 叫ぶ.
meaningMnemonic: 叫ぶ is "to shout" and "to scream." This is the noun version. This is a <vocabulary>shout</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>scream</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Neglect</kanji> someone so much that you remove yourself from their inner circle and live <kanji>outside</kanji> of their life and it's called <vocabulary>estrangement</vocabulary>. You might never see them again. But that's okay with you, your relationship is too weird to fix now.

readingMnemonic: It's working, it's working! The stick is returning to its <kanji>former</kanji> state and... w-wuh? It sprouted a <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう).
meaningMnemonic: There’s a <radical>stick</radical> next to the <radical>sun</radical>, reflecting on its <kanji>former</kanji> glory. The stick used to be a great tree, and the stick thinks that if it stays by the sun long enough it might return to its former form as a towering tree.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> <kanji>dance</kanji> <kanji>deed</kanji> is a deed you do that involves singing and dancing. This is the traditional form of stage deeds, known as <vocabulary>kabuki</vocabulary>. Watch it on YouTube if you want a taste.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 手 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

To be a good <vocabulary>pitcher</vocabulary>, all you have to do is put the ball into the <reading>chute</reading> (しゅ). Pitchers don't actually throw the ball. There is an invisible pitching chute right on the mound. You slide the ball into the chute and off it goes!
meaningMnemonic: You already know that 手 means "hand," but it can also mean "doer," as in someone who performs a particular action or task. Why? Because we use our hands to do things. And when it comes to <kanji>throw</kanji>ing, the <kanji>doer</kanji> is the <vocabulary>pitcher</vocabulary>!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
How do you represent an <kanji>equal</kanji> <kanji>number</kanji>? With an <vocabulary>equal sign</vocabulary>.

It's worth pointing out that this is a pretty formal word that's used in advanced math. In everyday conversation, people would use イコール for the equal sign.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Not</kanji> <kanji>pure</kanji> things are <vocabulary>impure</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
When you <kanji>help</kanji> with what you <kanji>say</kanji>, you're giving <vocabulary>advice</vocabulary>.

This word is commonly found in formal or professional contexts. In more casual settings, you can just use アドバイス (advise) instead.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you want to become a <kanji>martyr</kanji> during your <kanji>employment</kanji> you need to <vocabulary>die at your post</vocabulary>. I don't know why you'd WANT to do that though.

readingMnemonic: The grain of rice thinks about its former life as a <kanji>rice plant</kanji> and, like you, mutters "<reading>いね</reading>." What's that, little rice grain? Are you trying to say life was good?
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>grain</radical> stuck in your <radical>cleat</radical> had a <radical>former</radical> life. In that life it was a <kanji>rice plant</kanji>. It was a happy little rice plant, minding its own business, when it was yanked up, cleaned, and put in a bag for people to buy and cook and eat. That was so long ago. Now all that's left is this sad loose grain in the bottom of your shoe.

readingMnemonic:
You need someone who will <kanji>suit</kanji> you. Someone who can <kanji>join</kanji> you on your life journey. So you call Grandpa <reading>ごう</reading>いち.

Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち.
meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>suit</radical> and the kanji <kanji>suit</kanji> are exactly the same! This kanji can also mean <kanji>join</kanji> which makes sense. When something suits you well, like a hat or something, it joins together with you quite well too. Join me, my hat! You suit my head well. It just <kanji>fit</kanji>s, you know?
This is the radical for <radical>child</radical>. Aww, see how they're wearing a cap and have their little arms stretched out? You can almost hear them saying "pick me up!" A very child-like child.

readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you want to find some <kanji>coarse</kanji> <kanji>salt</kanji> just dive in the sea and collect <vocabulary>sea salt</vocabulary>! The pieces are nice and big and lumpy, so you really taste it when you're cooking.

readingMnemonic: One of the seven things you <kanji>consign</kanji> over to this guy is a <reading>tack</reading> (たく). It’s the sharpest tack you’ve ever seen. You slide the tack down the slide. Good thing no one is on the slide now, sitting on that tack would hurt.
meaningMnemonic: They <radical>say</radical> if you put things on a <radical>slide</radical>, <radical>seven</radical> things to be exact, that’s the best way to <kanji>consign</kanji> goods to someone. They say if you consign seven things to someone, you should send them over on a slide. Slide ‘em on down. All seven of ‘em.

readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already, so you should know this too!
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: 焼き uses the reading you learned with the kanji. 肉 does too. Put them on the grill and enjoy!
meaningMnemonic: Nicely <kanji>bake</kanji>d <kanji>meat</kanji> is <vocabulary>grilled meat</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>yakiniku</vocabulary>. Mmm, yum! If you go to Japan look out for 焼肉 places (same meaning and reading). They're pretty tasty, if you're into meat at least.

readingMnemonic: The person who's holding the <vocabulary>spear</vocabulary> is a little <reading>hoe 子</reading>. It's a child who learned to fight with a hoe, and he's turned the hoe into a <vocabulary>spear</vocabulary> to fight with. Imagine him swinging his hoe spear around like a little dork.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If everyone is acting <kanji>solemn</kanji> and <kanji>strict</kanji> then you should probably pay special attention to the <vocabulary>gravity</vocabulary> of the situation you're in. Don't start playing the trumpet when you're supposed to be bowing your head!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Charcoal</kanji> <kanji>mineral</kanji> has been found! Time to dig a <vocabulary>coal mine</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>coal pit</vocabulary> to retrieve it!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Something that's <kanji>flat</kanji> and <kanji>equal</kanji> to everything around it, all those flat things around it, are <vocabulary>average</vocabulary>. They're the <vocabulary>mean</vocabulary> (same as average).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The しゃく gets shortened to しゃっ though, so beware. Just think of that like the little bit that you lost to the yakuza, because they weren't happy you didn't pay back your debt. *cut*
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>money</kanji> (and <kanji>gold</kanji>) you <kanji>borrow</kanji> is your <vocabulary>debt</vocabulary>. Be sure to pay it back before the yakuza come for you.

readingMnemonic: If you try <vocabulary>to hold something</vocabulary> in your hand long enough it will <reading>mo</reading>ld (も). And then that mold will cover your hand, then your arm, then your entire body. Basically, you should never hold anything for too long or you'll become a mold person.
meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>hold</kanji> and the verb version is <vocabulary>to hold something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to carry something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to own something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to keep something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. You hold something, like chopsticks, have something, like power, or keep something, like your friend's book over the weekend.

readingMnemonic: You go up to the <kanji>neglect</kanji>ed coat rack and try to make things right by cleaning it with <reading>so</reading>ap (そ). But no matter how much you scrub, it won't get clean, the arms won't go back on.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>coat rack</radical> will turn into a <radical>bundle</radical> of sticks if you <kanji>neglect</kanji> it. When you neglect a coat rack, the weight from the coats will pull all of the arms off, leaving it as a <kanji>sparse</kanji> stick.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>fruit</kanji> <kanji>wood</kanji> is what a fruit grows on (the wood of a fruit is a tree, dummy). That makes this word a <vocabulary>fruit tree</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: You have <kanji>flat object</kanji>s but <kanji>what</kanji> amount of flat objects? This word is asking that question: "<vocabulary>how many flat objects</vocabulary> are there?" If this doesn't make sense, think back to words like 何回 or 何年 which ask "how many ____" just like this one.

readingMnemonic:
The reading for 都 is an exception from what you learned with the kanji. To remember this, just think about someone who does something at their own convenience. They say, I'm going <reading>to go</reading> (つごう) where I want, when I want, at my own convenience.

The 合 (ごう) part is a reading you know from the kanji, though, so if you can get to "to go" with the mnemonic, you should be able to put two and two together to know that it's a long vowel ごう.

This verb is transitive, so it needs a direct object — you bewitch, trick, or deceive someone. You know this because when a fox wants to bewitch someone, they have to <reading>cuss</reading> (かす). They say a magic cuss word that lets them change forms and fool people. Those tricksy foxes…

This word is often used in a positive context for recommending things, actions, and people by implying or pointing out their charms, merits, or both.

Although 薦める and 勧める are similar, there are subtle differences between the two. 勧める is often used to suggest that someone perform a specific action, often as friendly advice or encouragement. It can also be used when offering something, such as a drink. On the other hand, 薦める is used to recommend a person or thing as suitable for a particular situation, with a focus on endorsing the subject rather than a specific action.

You've seen 起きる which is "to wake up." This is similar, except you are waking someone else up, which makes the meaning of this word <vocabulary>to wake someone up</vocabulary>. How do you differentiate between this and 起きる? Because of the す on the end. You wake someone up violently, wrenching their neck. They turn around and <reading>sue</reading> (す) you, making you wish you never woke them up.

This can also mean <vocabulary>to cause something</vocabulary>. I guess if you wake someone up and they're not a morning person, you could cause something... like trouble.

meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Equal</kanji> out your <kanji>equilibrium</kanji> and you'll have solid <vocabulary>equilibrium</vocabulary>.

As is often our recommendation for more complicated or hard-to-translate words like this one, check out our common word combinations and context sentences to see how this word is used!

The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

You've been waiting <vocabulary>for a while</vocabulary> and nothing has happened yet, so you start singing a <reading>shee</reading>p <reading>balla</reading>d (しばら). This ballad helps you sleep by counting sheep. If you manage to doze off <vocabulary>for some time</vocabulary>, time will surely pass faster, and then something might happen!

When you do something <kanji>temporarily</kanji>, you're only doing it <vocabulary>for a while</vocabulary>. It's not permanent — however long it lasts, it's just <vocabulary>for some time</vocabulary>.

暫く refers to a stretch of time that's not too long, but not super short either — just somewhere in between. How long, exactly? It kinda depends on the speaker. If it feels like a while to you, then hey, it's a while!

Keep in mind that the kanji form is quite formal, so it's more commonly written in kana, like しばらく.

To remember that this kanji is the repeater, though, think of a <radical>prison</radical> with <radical>drop</radical>s of water dripping over and over in it. Drip drop drip drop. It does that over and over again, driving the prisoners nuts. But it never stops. It just repeats over and over.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The 説 gets shortened to せっ.
meaningMnemonic: You <kanji>acquire</kanji> <kanji>theory</kanji> after theory. In doing this, you have a lot of theories in your head. readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

readingMnemonic:

<vocabulary>Every month</vocabulary>, you make <reading>two</reading> <reading>key</reading>s (つき). Why? Imagine you're a key maker, and two keys is your <vocabulary>monthly</vocabulary> quota. It's a very light key quota, two keys, but that's why you're able to hit it every month.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Every</kanji> <kanji>moon</kanji> is <vocabulary>every month</vocabulary> (as you know from all the month-related vocab). This can also mean <vocabulary>monthly</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 月 has two on'yomi readings, and the reading here changes from げつ to げっ, here's a mnemonic to help you remember how to read this one:

Legend has it that the <vocabulary>moonlight</vocabulary> brings out a creature known as the <reading>Geck光</reading> (げっこう), an elusive species of gecko that shines in the moonlight.
