Everyone thinks you're crazy, but you know you'll find that Geck光 someday!
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> <kanji>light</kanji> is exactly what it sounds like: it's <vocabulary>moonlight</vocabulary>! This word can also refer to a <vocabulary>moonbeam</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This kanji uses the kun'yomi read for the first kanji, and the on'yomi reading for the second. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this too.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>float</kanji>ing <kanji>spirit</kanji>? If your spirit is floating around (in matters of love), then you might be likely to <vocabulary>cheat</vocabulary> on your partner. Careful — once it starts, your <vocabulary>cheating</vocabulary> could turn into a full-blown <vocabulary>affair</vocabulary>.

浮気 means cheating in a relationship, whether you're dating or married. But even harmless flirting can sometimes count as 浮気, since it indicates your spirit is "floating" and not as securely tied to your partner as they'd like…

readingMnemonic: <kanji>Seaweed</kanji> is true <reading>sou</reading>l (そう) food. Which means it's good for your soul. Didn't you ever read those books about chicken soup being good for your soul? Well that was a lie. Miso soup with seaweed is what's really good for your soul.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>flowers</radical> that wash up on shore in <radical>tsunami</radical>s that we make into <radical>syrup</radical> is <kanji>seaweed</kanji>. Okay, so it's more like soup or tea than syrup, but you can make them both out of seaweed.

readingMnemonic: Walking down the <kanji>beach</kanji> a bit more, you also find a <reading>hammer</reading> (はま). Gosh, looks like the tsunami hit a workshop or a hardware store or something. First the axe, now a hammer.
meaningMnemonic: After a <radical>tsunami</radical>, you find an <radical>axe</radical> on the <radical>ground</radical> next to some <radical>fins</radical> on the <kanji>beach</kanji>. The tsunami was pretty violent, and it looks like this axe got blown into some fish and cut off their fins and now those things are just on the ground by the beach.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>sick</kanji> <kanji>institution</kanji> is a place where sick people go. That is a <vocabulary>hospital</vocabulary>.

病院 is a broad word used to talk about not just big hospitals but also regular <vocabulary>doctor's office</vocabulary>s or <vocabulary>clinic</vocabulary>s. So when Japanese people speak English, they might say "hospital" even when they are just going to a small, local clinic.

readingMnemonic: Ready, steady, <kanji>aim</kanji>... fire! You throw a bar of <reading>so</reading>ap (そ) at the animal. Yes, soap. You were sitting in your bathtub, washing and scrubbing, then the animal in the top hat caught your eye.
meaningMnemonic: You see an <radical>animal</radical> wearing a <radical>top hat</radical> and decide to <kanji>aim</kanji> at it. The top hat is a perfect, giant target you use to take down this animal.

readingMnemonic: Do you know that movie, <reading>Tetsu</reading>o (てつ) the <kanji>Iron</kanji> Man? We talked about it on Tofugu a while back. It’s one of the wackiest Japanese movies of all time. If you don’t know about Tetsuo the Iron Man, you should definitely look it up (if you aren't averse to horror/violent films). Tetsuo is one of the most insane movies in the history of ever.
meaningMnemonic: You look at some <radical>gold</radical> and notice a <radical>fault</radical> in it. You scrape at the fault and see that it's just sprayed with gold paint. It's not gold, it's (comparatively) worthless <kanji>iron</kanji>!

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!
meaningMnemonic:
This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>celebrate</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>celebration</vocabulary>! 

お祝い is also used to mean a <vocabulary>congratulatory gift</vocabulary> itself.

readingMnemonic: Eventually, your friends and family find you at the cliff, tripping on tofu. Each and every <kanji>vein</kanji> on your body is engorged, pulsating with the effects of tofu. Your friends try and take you home. "You cyan't <reading>myake</reading> (みゃく) me!" you slur, suffering from the effects of the tofu. "None of you cyan myake me go home! You cyan’t myake me! Nyah!"
meaningMnemonic: Under the <radical>moon</radical> while you sit on a <radical>cliff</radical>, you inject a syringe of <radical>tofu</radical> right into your <kanji>vein</kanji>. Ahh, tofu. You're addicted to it. You sneak out to the cliff at night to get your tofu fix, injecting it straight into your vein.

readingMnemonic: This word has hiragana attached to the kanji, which is a good sign that the reading is kun'yomi. You learned that reading when you learned the kanji, so you should be good to go.
meaningMnemonic:
You know that the kanji 田 means <kanji>rice paddy</kanji>, so it should be easy to work out that this word also means <vocabulary>rice paddy</vocabulary>.

田んぼ is a common way to say "rice paddy," especially in casual conversation. You can tell because if you ever came across a ju<reading>mbo</reading> (んぼ) rice paddy, you'd probably say something like, "Whoa, that's one jumbo 田んぼ!" When a 田んぼ is that jumbo, the surprise makes your speech naturally more relaxed and informal.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 検査 already as well.
meaningMnemonic: You know that 検査 is inspection, so the verb version of that would be <vocabulary>to inspect</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji and with 腫れる, so you should be alright here.
meaningMnemonic: You know that 腫れる means "to swell," and this is the noun version: <vocabulary>swelling</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the two kun'yomi vocab readings combined. So, 穴 and 子 to combine make あなご. Just watch out for rendaku, which changes the reading of 子 from こ to ご.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>hole</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> isn't some kind of creepy hole child (not sure how else to describe it). It's a <vocabulary>conger eel</vocabulary>, a type of tasty eel eaten in Japan. It might be easier to learn the reading first, though, and use that, because the second meaning option is <vocabulary>anago</vocabulary>, the Japanese word for it (also used in English).

readingMnemonic: Mostly, though, the  <kanji>juvenile</kanji>s are standing on top of village buildings, eating <reading>dou</reading>ghnuts (どう).
meaningMnemonic: Those who <radical>stand</radical> on top of a <radical>village</radical> are <kanji>juvenile</kanji>. Imagine a bunch of young people standing on the roofs of buildings in the village. That's a juvenile thing to do.

readingMnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (see that hiragana?) but that's the reading you learned with the kanji. Enjoy the ride!
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>ride</kanji> so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to ride</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Think about your <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary> even if you don't have one. What's his name? It's <reading>Otto</reading> (おっと), and he's always leaving you at home because he's working at the <reading>auto</reading> (おっと) shop.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that smooshes two previous vocabulary words together into a new one. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: An "examination hell" is the nickname given to the exams you have to take in Japan all at once. That's why this is <vocabulary>exam hell</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. Because the reading sounds just like a dirty word, and there may be innocent children about, I'll let you come up with your own mnemonic for this one. Maybe someone pushes you into a deep hole that will surely kill you so you yell something out as you fall down it?
meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>deep</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>deep</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Then you decide to <kanji>put</kanji> <reading>chee</reading>se (ち) in your net. With a perfectly straight net and the cheese you put down as bait, there’s no way this fails. Success is all about how you put the net down and the cheese you put in it.
meaningMnemonic: You need your <radical>net</radical> to be <radical>straight</radical> before you <kanji>put</kanji> it on the ground and try to lure something into it. You put your net there to catch something, but if it's twisted or tangled, it won't be very effective.

readingMnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi reading which you learned with 遠い. How convenient!
meaningMnemonic: This is the noun/no-adjective version of the kanji <kanji>far</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>far away</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>distant</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: A ton of <kanji>rice</kanji> is grown in <kanji>America</kanji>. And yet you never see rice in American cuisine. So where's all that unused rice going? Actually, it all gets dumped into a big <reading>bay</reading> (べい). They have too much rice and no place to store it, so they've started using bays to store it.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>rice</radical> radical and <kanji>rice</kanji> kanji are the same in looks and meaning. This kanji can also mean <kanji>America</kanji>, maybe because America is covered in rice or fields or something?

readingMnemonic: You just had the doctor <kanji>diagnose</kanji> you with hair loss. How terrible! You stumble out of the room, dumbfounded. Not paying attention, you bang your <reading>shin</reading> (しん) on the table. Your shin really hurts. What an awful day.
meaningMnemonic: They <radical>say</radical> to wear a <radical>hat</radical> to cover your <radical>hair</radical> if your doctor <kanji>diagnose</kanji>s you with hair loss. It's the best option, folks.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Only for you, when you visit <reading>Nara</reading> (なら), the deer there are <vocabulary>to be lined up</vocabulary> for you to inspect, as you are the deer inspector. If you don't know about Nara and its deer, you should look it up, they're pretty awesome.
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>line up</kanji>, and this is the intransitive verb version of that, which makes this <vocabulary>to line up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be lined up</vocabulary>. You can remember this because you keep saying <reading>boo</reading> (ぶ), why is everyone already lined up? If you were the one in charge of lining things up, you wouldn't have <vocabulary>to stand in line</vocabulary> yourself…

Figuratively, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be on par</vocabulary>, as in someone or something matches or is comparable in ability, status, or ranking to another (as if they are aligned side by side in comparison).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: You receive <kanji>profit</kanji> at every <kanji>breath</kanji>. What kind of profit is this? It's <vocabulary>interest</vocabulary>. As time goes by and as you take more breaths you gain more bank interest.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Something that is <kanji>public</kanji>ly <kanji>manage</kanji>d is something that is <vocabulary>public</vocabulary> aka <vocabulary>government run</vocabulary>. Compare this to 私営 which is private / privately run.

readingMnemonic: The readings are the on'yomi readings. You've learned them both already, good for you!
meaningMnemonic: Use your <kanji>finger</kanji> to <kanji>indicate</kanji> some things. These are your <vocabulary>instructions</vocabulary>. Okay, do this (point), do that (point), and then finally do this (point).

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

As you're looking at <vocabulary>job posting</vocabulary>s, you notice they're all looking for people with <reading>cu</reading>cumbers and <reading>jean</reading>s (きゅうじん). That's the only qualification they're after, cucumbers and jeans.
meaningMnemonic: When you're <kanji>request</kanji>ing <kanji>people</kanji>, you put up a <vocabulary>job posting</vocabulary> because you’re <vocabulary>seeking workers</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is an exception, but you learned it with the kanji. Congratulations!
meaningMnemonic: If you do something <kanji>gradually</kanji> for a long time, when you finish it gives you that <vocabulary>FINALLY</vocabulary> feeling. It took so long and you worked so hard and you're finally done!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. 楽 has two on'yomi readings, but you know it's がく here because it's about 音楽 (music)!
meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 管弦楽 means "orchestral music?" Well the <kanji>group</kanji> that plays that music is an <vocabulary>orchestra</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
You can also <kanji>seal</kanji> <reading>foo</reading>d (ふう) in dirt to make it last longer. That's how jerky came about, you know. Seal some meat underground and in a few months you'll have some tasty dried meats to chew.

By the way, this has another reading you should probably know. It's ほう. Most sealing is done in the <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう), you know? So just think about eating food in your own home!
meaningMnemonic: You take two clumps of <radical>dirt</radical> to make a <radical>measurement</radical>, using them to <kanji>seal</kanji> each side of your measuring tape, so it stays on the ground. This is the way people used to <kanji>seal in</kanji> things back in the day, back when we didn't have fancy things like tape and glue.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "You going <vocabulary>to attack</vocabulary> me or something? <reading>Oh so</reading> scary you are. Oh so scary. Ho ho ho."
meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>attack</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to attack</vocabulary>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>wide</radical>.

readingMnemonic: I also do all my <kanji>hunt</kanji>s using a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). I just run those animals down with my car. Kind of cheating, but vroom vroom anyways.
meaningMnemonic: I <radical>protect</radical> my own <radical>animal</radical>s by going to <kanji>hunt</kanji> other animals... like wolves and cougars and such.

readingMnemonic: You learned this reading already when you learned 迷う! Just swap the う for an い.
meaningMnemonic:
Remember how you learned that 迷う means "to go astray" or "to get lost?" Well, when you feel like you've gone astray or gotten lost, you might act with <vocabulary>hesitation</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>indecision</vocabulary>. You suddenly have <vocabulary>doubt</vocabulary> about where to go or what to do next.

While 迷う can mean getting lost either physically or mentally, 迷い most often conveys an abstract sense of inner conflict or uncertainty, especially in decision making.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
An <kanji>occurrence</kanji> of some <kanji>matter</kanji> is really just something that happens. It's an <vocabulary>incident</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>case</vocabulary>. 

事件 often refers to significant or serious occurrences like crime cases or accidents. It can also be used playfully — "There was a 事件 at the party!" — to dramatize an event like someone asking out your classmate.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>confused</kanji> <kanji>riot</kanji> causes even more <vocabulary>confusion</vocabulary>. Soon there will be so many <vocabulary>distraction</vocabulary>s happening, what with cars tipping over and fires starting, that no one will know which way is up!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>next</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji> you look at this kanji, you should know that it means <vocabulary>next time</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>origin</kanji> of your <kanji>foundation</kanji> is where you have to work from when learning something new. For example, the 基本 portions of WaniKani are the earlier levels, especially the radicals. They are the <vocabulary>foundation</vocabulary> you need to learn your kanji and vocab later on.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Nourishing</kanji> and <kanji>foster</kanji>ing. The thing that gives you this is <vocabulary>nourishment</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>nutrition</vocabulary>.

滋養 is a formal and somewhat old-fashioned word. It's mostly used in writing to describe nutritious foods or the health benefits of supplements, tonics, or energy drinks.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
Once you've <kanji>solve</kanji>d a <kanji>theory</kanji>, you should be able to give a pretty good <vocabulary>explanation</vocabulary> of it to somebody else. Makes sense, right? 

解説 refers to a detailed and analytical explanation. It's often used when someone, often an expert, provides an in-depth analysis about a topic, like a sports game or news article <vocabulary>commentary</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The ざつ goes to ざっ and the ひ goes to ぴ, making it into a dumb sounding word, like "zappy" (ざっぴ), so you can think about how some of your miscellaneous expenses were on zappy items.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Random</kanji> <kanji>expense</kanji>s are <vocabulary>miscellaneous expenses</vocabulary>. Not actually random, but they feel that way.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. You may have to think back to some other words using 投 to remember the on'yomi reading, 投資 for example.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Throw</kanji> a <kanji>ballot</kanji> in the ballot box <vocabulary>to vote</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with 直す, but here's a mnemonic in case you forgot:

Something needs <vocabulary>to be fixed</vocabulary> <reading>now</reading> (なお)! Seriously, it's urgent! You need this thing <vocabulary>to be back in working order</vocabulary> right now!
meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 直す means "to fix," where someone actively does the fixing. Well, 直る puts the focus on the thing getting fixed, so it means <vocabulary>to be fixed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be back in working order</vocabulary>.

In other words, don't use it to say "I fixed it," but do use it to say "It's fixed!" or "It's back to normal!" To remember this, imagine a British person excitedly shouting, "My loo (る) was broken, but now it's fixed!”
meanings: To Be Back In Working Order

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: An <kanji>aviation</kanji> (航空) <kanji>mother</kanji> <kanji>warship</kanji> is a warship that is like mother to all the aviation things (the airplanes). They come home to their mother warship, which is an <vocabulary>aircraft carrier</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
If you <kanji>crash</kanji> and <kanji>fall</kanji> then you're <vocabulary>crashing</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>falling</vocabulary>, or maybe both.

墜落 refers to falling from a height and ending with a crash, like an airplane or a satellite plummeting to the ground.

readingMnemonic: Like other verbs that end in じる, this actually uses the on'yomi of the kanji, not kun'yomi! You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go here.
meaningMnemonic:
You have <kanji>pass through</kanji>, so this is <vocabulary>to pass through</vocabulary>.

This word has a bunch of different meanings, and translations will vary depending on context. In short, it's mostly used figuratively to mean that something, like communication, is passing or coming through successfully. Have a look at our common word combinations and context sentences for some example usages!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 経済 as well.
meaningMnemonic: You know how 経済 is economics, right? Well, add <kanji>study</kanji> to that and you have the study of economics, aka <vocabulary>economics</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: A <kanji>storm</kanji> is nothing to scoff at. If you get hit by the storm and get all wet and nasty and electrocuted, you're bound to get <reading>a rash</reading> (あらし).
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>mountain</radical> <radical>wind</radical> coming down from the mountains is very fierce. It is so fierce it's a lot like a <kanji>storm</kanji>. Well, it is a storm, really.

readingMnemonic: You end up saying, "You should <kanji>visit</kanji> my <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう)." How kind of you!
meaningMnemonic: Someone just asked you to <radical>say</radical> which <radical>direction</radical> they should <kanji>visit</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: You need this specific <kanji>paper</kanji> to prove that you aren't a <reading>Commi</reading> (かみ), aka a Communist. Or that you are. It really depends on where you want to go and what decade this is.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>thread</radical> that ties you to your <radical>clan</radical> is <kanji>paper</kanji>. Your papers, that is.

readingMnemonic:
The reading is that of the word 出る and the word 会う, both of which you've hopefully seen. The 出 portion may be confusing, but you can usually assume that if one part of the word is kun'yomi / vocab reading, the other part is too, which is why 出 uses the vocab reading.

So, the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to bake</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to burn something</vocabulary>, or even <vocabulary>to grill</vocabulary>.

焼く means to apply heat to something to change it in a physical way. It can refer to lightly toasting something, charring it, or even burning it to ashes depending on the context. It's commonly used in cooking contexts to describe baking, grilling, or roasting food. But it can also be used with pottery, film photography, and even sun-tanning.

This is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object. But 受ける often implies passive reception, generally of intangible objects like an education, or damage. It can also mean <vocabulary>to take something</vocabulary>, like taking an exam or a job offer.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

This training allows you to become super human. You go beyond the limits of a normal human. You become a human who can run really fast.

readingMnemonic: These <kanji>beans</kanji> are from <reading>とう</reading>きょう. Everybody knows とうきょう has the best beans. What?! You didn’t know that? Tokyo’s beans are the best beans!

Remember how 忘れる is "to forget"? Well, a <kanji>thing</kanji> you've forgotten is a <vocabulary>forgotten item</vocabulary>.

忘れ物 is a casual way to refer to something left behind accidentally, like an umbrella you forgot about and left on the train.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Luck</kanji> for your whole <kanji>lifespan</kanji>, that's a life of <vocabulary>happiness and longevity</vocabulary>.

少女 is a relatively formal word that's often used in writing to describe a <vocabulary>young girl</vocabulary>, usually between childhood and adolescence (or between the ages of about five and eighteen).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>enter</kanji> <kanji>prison</kanji> that's <vocabulary>imprisonment</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>pig</kanji>'s <kanji>meat</kanji> is called <vocabulary>pork</vocabulary>.

meaningMnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji and has the same meaning as well: <vocabulary>coloring</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know the word 否定 as well.
meaningMnemonic: If 否定 is "denial," then the verb version would be <vocabulary>to deny</vocabulary>.

A 間違い is a mistake. A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>mistake</kanji> is a <vocabulary>big mistake</vocabulary>.

大間違い is less about factual errors and more about someone being way off in their assumptions or expectations. It suggests things didn't go according to plan — like you assumed a smile would fix everything or expected a date to go well, only for things to turn out completely wrong.

readingMnemonic:
This isn’t the reading you learned with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You don’t just get irritated, you get <reading>ira-ira</reading>-tated (いらいら). That's the next level up from irritated.

This word is often written in katakana or hiragana, but you'll sometimes see it in kanji too, so it's worth knowing!
meaningMnemonic: Double <kanji>frustration</kanji> would cause anyone <vocabulary>to get irritated</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get annoyed</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to grow impatient</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

Note when you stick this onto another word to specify a type of sugar, like きび砂糖 (cane sugar), this gets rendaku'd to ざとう.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>sand</kanji> <kanji>sugar</kanji> is just <vocabulary>sugar</vocabulary>.  Nom nom nom, sugar.

readingMnemonic: The reading is 熊's reading, the alternate "origin" 本 reading, and the reading for 県.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Bear</kanji> <kanji>origin</kanji> <kanji>prefecture</kanji> is <vocabulary>Kumamoto Prefecture</vocabulary>. Probably best to learn this meaning via the reading. Also, you should look up Kumamon of Kumamoto-ken.

readingMnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji, but it uses the on'yomi reading, not the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you've learned this reading already. Yay!
meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

甲 has traditionally meant <vocabulary>turtle shell</vocabulary>, but these days it appears much more often in expressions like 足の甲 (<vocabulary>instep</vocabulary>) and 手の甲 (<vocabulary>back of the hand</vocabulary>). If you think about it, those body parts kind of resemble turtle shells, don’t you think?

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji>'s <kanji>nature</kanji> is just <vocabulary>human nature</vocabulary>! Everyone has their own human <vocabulary>instinct</vocabulary>s.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: An <kanji>elderly</kanji> <kanji>old woman</kanji> is just an <vocabulary>old woman</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wet</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to get wet</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The person you <kanji>help</kanji> with your top hat power? It's <reading>Jo</reading>-Anne (じょ).
meaningMnemonic: With <radical>top hat</radical> <radical>power</radical>, you're able to <kanji>help</kanji> anyone.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Knowing 消化 and 不良 will help as well.
meaningMnemonic: You've hopefully seen 消化 by now and know that it means "digestion." If you know that, then you can see that the "digestion" is <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>good</kanji>. When your digestion is not good, what do you have? <vocabulary>Indigestion</vocabulary>. Excuse me, I have to run to the restroom...

readingMnemonic:
The reading is the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn. In order to learn it, think of this:

I <vocabulary>always</vocabulary> <reading>tune</reading> (つね) my violin, but today I didn't tune it. So, now I sound terrible. Imagine how terrible my untuned violin sounds, compared to how it always sounds.
meaningMnemonic: The particle に here is a clue that this word is an adverb. An adverb describes actions, so what's a <kanji>normal</kanji> action? It's one you're <vocabulary>always</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>constantly</vocabulary>, doing. That's what makes it normal!

readingMnemonic: What are you in <kanji>deliberation</kanji> about? Whether or not to send some poor soul to the <reading>gui</reading>llotine (ぎ). "I think he should go," you say. "I don't think he should," says another. This <kanji>deliberation</kanji> is going nowhere...
meaningMnemonic: What you <radical>say</radical> is <radical>righteousness</radical>, at least that's what you believe. You keep talking and saying these things, and you don't listen to anyone else's words. This is your style of <kanji>deliberation</kanji> and <kanji>discussion</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: I will <kanji>judge</kanji> and <kanji>inspect</kanji> you. This is an <vocabulary>examination</vocabulary>, so we'll see if you pass.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

See the slide going into the dirt? What appears to be a slide here is actually a <radical>coffin</radical>, sliding into the dirt to be buried.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>navigation</kanji> <kanji>method</kanji>s are the methods used for <vocabulary>navigation</vocabulary>.

航法 is a technical term for navigation, specifically referring to the techniques and methods used to guide a ship, aircraft, or spacecraft from one place to another.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Something that's <kanji>outside</kanji> the <kanji>example</kanji> doesn't follow the rules. It's not what it's supposed to be (the example), it is the <vocabulary>exception</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: To learn the reading, just think about how you're looking at something for a lonnnnng time if you're staring at it. In Japanese the word "long" is 長い, and guess what the reading of the kanji part is? It's なが, just like <reading>なが</reading>める's kanji-part reading.
meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stare</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to stare at</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>to look at</vocabulary> in a very staringish way).

readingMnemonic:
This word has two different meanings and each one has its own reading.

When it's used for <vocabulary>corner</vocabulary>s, the reading is かど. Just picture a deck of <reading>card</reading>s (かど). What's the most important part of the card? The corner! The corners are where the numbers are. Now tape those cards into all the corners of your house. Why? Because it's artsy!

And the second meaning and reading pair is easy — <vocabulary>angle</vocabulary> and かく, which you already know from the kanji!
meaningMnemonic:
When the kanji for <kanji>angle</kanji> is used as a standalone word, it usually means <vocabulary>corner</vocabulary>. You can remember this because corners are pretty much the most common kind of angle you see in everyday life.

In math contexts, it can also mean <vocabulary>angle</vocabulary> — just like the kanji's meaning!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>surface</kanji> that <kanji>accumulate</kanji>s into one area is a particular <vocabulary>area</vocabulary>. This has to do with math. When you add all the surfaces together by accumulating them into one calculation, you get yourself the area!

readingMnemonic: The dirt-covered head asks for help <kanji>again</kanji> and again, but you've only got a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). So you start digging with it, scraping the dirt away, until you see this head has the body of a <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい)!
meaningMnemonic: Under the <radical>ground</radical>, a <radical>head</radical> covered in <radical>dirt</radical> emerges... <kanji>again</kanji>! It's not the first time you've seen this buried head, nor is it the last. This dirt-covered head hides beneath the ground wherever you go, and keeps popping up to scare you again and again.

readingMnemonic: The reading is just the kun'yomi reading (which you learned with the kanji) twice in a row.
meaningMnemonic: You give your <kanji>congratulations</kanji> to someone a few times because they seem so <vocabulary>fresh</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>vibrant</vocabulary>. You feel like you should because it must be nice to be like that still. Someday it will be gone, so make sure you say it a few times right away.

readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: You head out into the <kanji>public</kanji> where everyone can see your fins, but... things have changed. All people are the same. There are thousands of <reading>こう</reading>いちs walking around, and they all stare at you (though they pretend like they aren't).
meaningMnemonic: You have <radical>fins</radical> in <radical>private</radical>. But, you want the world to see them, so you take them <kanji>public</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>punish</kanji> <kanji>period of time</kanji> is the time in which you are being punished in prison. This is your <vocabulary>prison term</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Some <kanji>odd</kanji> <kanji>traces</kanji> are left over here. We don't really understand what happened, because it was a <vocabulary>miracle</vocabulary>, but it certainly left some odd traces behind.

To remember the reading い we use the word "eagle." 

You're trying <vocabulary>to say</vocabulary> something, but every time you try to say anything an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) swoops down and pecks at your face then flies away. Just imagine yourself saying tiny bits of words, then an eagle crashing down on your face. Then, you wait in silence. Nothing happens. You try to say something again, and the eagle swoops down on you again.
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>say</kanji>, so the verb version of that is <vocabulary>to say</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Help</kanji> and <kanji>aid</kanji> someone and you will <vocabulary>help</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>aid</vocabulary> them! Good job, you're a good person.

readingMnemonic:
You already learned this reading when you learned 点ける but here's a mnemonic just in case:

Every time you count to <reading>two</reading> (つ) a light comes on. How cool that it does it all by itself!!
meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji 点 means <kanji>point</kanji>, but this verb actually means <vocabulary>to be lit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be ignited</vocabulary>. Think of it this way, when a flashlight turns on, it points a beam, of light.

You already learned 点ける, which is for when you turn something on. 点く, on the other hand, is an intransitive verb. That means it happens by itself. Like, "Oh look! The lights came on! That's <reading>cool</reading> (く)!"

readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them when you learned the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 渡す means "to hand over?" Well you can use your actual <kanji>hand</kanji> <vocabulary>to hand over</vocabulary> something too!

readingMnemonic: To get to the best <kanji>fishing</kanji> spot you need to <reading>go</reading> (ぎょ) <reading>row</reading> (りょう) out to the middle of the ocean. You go by means of rowing. To get to the fish and do the fishing, you need to go and row out to sea.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> pushes all the <radical>fish</radical> closer to land, making for some easy <kanji>fishing</kanji>. The tsunami starts out in the middle of the ocean and pushes all the fish towards the coast where everyone does their fishing. With all the fish pushed closer to land and closer together, it’s very easy for people to go fishing in one spot and catch a lot of fish.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Think of all the things you start <vocabulary>to despise</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to disdain</vocabulary>. Now come up with some <reading>anecdo</reading>tes (あなど) for each one of those things. Be sure to think in your head, "I'm coming up with anecdotes for things I disdain, why am I coming up with anecdotes?"
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>despise</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to despise</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: You're almost done <kanji>eras</kanji>ing your fingers when the jet starts sucking all of you in. You would try to grab the closest thing to you, but your fingers don't exist anymore, so you hold onto the <reading>mats</reading> (まつ) at your feet with your toes. The mats are super strong (they're made for jets, after all) and you manage to save yourself!
meaningMnemonic: Put your <radical>fingers</radical> in a <radical>jet</radical> if you want to <kanji>erase</kanji> them from existence. You aren't just chopping or burning them off. There's like, no trace of them at all. Your parents can't even remember if you were born with fingers or not. Jets are that powerful.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you've seen before. The かぜ reading is the same one you learned with the vocab word 風, so if you can remember that you should have no trouble with this word!
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>south</kanji> <kanji>wind</kanji> is… a <vocabulary>south wind</vocabulary>!

南風 is a wind that blows from the south. In Japan it's associated with the warmer temperatures it carries up from the tropics.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>wander</kanji> around doing nothing at your own <kanji>expense</kanji> it will be a huge <vocabulary>waste</vocabulary> of money. It's not like you were doing or buying anything important, you were just wandering around, after all.

This looks like someone in a standing position with legs planted firmly on the ground, spreading their arms out in a T-pose to maintain balance. So that makes this the radical for <radical>stand</radical>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is obi (おび), so if you know the meaning, you know the reading as well! If you need an extra reminder, ask yourself "What is the first letter in belt?" Hmm, I can't remember. <reading>OH! "B"</reading> (おび)! I remember now.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are the same, except that this isn't just any type of <kanji>belt</kanji>. It's an <vocabulary>obi</vocabulary>, a wide cloth <vocabulary>belt</vocabulary> worn with traditional clothes like kimono and yukata.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
I <kanji>recommend</kanji> this to you, so I'd like to <kanji>invite</kanji> you to try it. This is a <vocabulary>solicitation</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>invitation</vocabulary>.

勧誘 means soliciting someone to buy a product or service or inviting them to join a group or activity, often in a pushy way. It's commonly used to describe what telemarketers and door-to-door evangelists do, or for students recruiting new members for extracurricular activities.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Fiber</kanji>s that have been <kanji>change</kanji>d from other materials are <vocabulary>synthetic fibers</vocabulary>. They aren't natural because they were something else once. Like plastic, or kittens.

Note that this is an abbreviation of the specialist term 化学繊維, and it mostly comes up in industrial contexts.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
Remember how 庶民 means "common people"? Well, anything that's "common-people-<kanji>like</kanji>" is <vocabulary>ordinary</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>unpretentious</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>approachable</vocabulary>.

Unlike 庶民, which can sometimes have negative connotations, 庶民的 is usually positive. It's used for things that appeal to ordinary people, like an unpretentious restaurant or a person with a familiar, approachable vibe.

readingMnemonic: This car is probably so <kanji>soft</kanji> because it's made entirely of <reading>naan</reading> (なん). Naan may be delicious, but it makes a really crappy car. No wonder it was so soft (and yummy).
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>car</radical> that's <radical>lack</radical>ing is really <kanji>soft</kanji>. Cars need to be hard so that things like bugs and other cars wont hurt the people inside when you hit them. But if your car is lacking the hardness it needs, you'll have a really soft, useless car.

Wondering about the difference between 代わる and 替わる? 代わる is used when someone or something takes the place of another, like filling in for a sick coworker. Whereas 替わる is used when things or situations switch places or are replaced with something new, like when talking about generations changing or a new governmental cabinet taking over.

This verb is intransitive, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. You'll sometimes see it with the particle を, though, because the を is showing a "path" rather than a direct object in this case. For example, 席を替わる (to switch seats) indicates your location is moving from one seat to another. Likewise, 電話を替わる indicates that a call is being handed off to another person.

meaningMnemonic: You have at your disposal a <radical>tsunami</radical> to assassinate this <radical>person</radical>, or a <radical>hook</radical>. Which method will you choose? <kanji>Decide</kanji> now!

readingMnemonic: You lie down and try to figure out what the <kanji>cloud</kanji>s are shaped like. The first cloud is shaped... like a <reading>coo</reading>l <reading>mo</reading>m (くも). readingMnemonic:
Things seem <vocabulary>to get dirty</vocabulary> easily around here, which is why <reading>you go</reading> (よご) to great lengths to keep things clean.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>dirty</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to get dirty</vocabulary>. You know you're not doing the dirtying, because it's <reading>rare</reading> (れる) for you to get anything dirty, though things do get dirty on their own.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Something that is <kanji>ultra</kanji> natural (自然的) is <vocabulary>supernatural</vocabulary>. Too natural! Super!

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading when you learned 揺る, 揺する, and 揺れる so I reeeeally hope you can remember it by now!
meaningMnemonic: Hey look! If you weren't sick of them yet, it's another verb that goes with <kanji>shake</kanji>! This one means <vocabulary>to shake</vocabulary> too!

readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>brushwood</kanji> <kanji>dog</kanji> is the <vocabulary>Shiba Inu</vocabulary>. They're the same pretty orange color as brushwood trees, so that's how they got their name.

readingMnemonic: You want your friend to <kanji>lend</kanji> you some money so you can buy yourself a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). You need money and a car a lot more than you need this pile of shellfish, so you’re happy to put them up as collateral for the loan.
meaningMnemonic: You <radical>substitute</radical> some <radical>shellfish</radical> for collateral so your friend will <kanji>lend</kanji> you some money. Normally he would ask for something more valuable, but you’ve convinced him to substitute these shellfish for what he would normally take as collateral when lending to people.

A (modified) prison radical containing a person radical. What does a person experience in prison? <radical>Lack</radical>. Prison is all about lack — lack of freedom, lack of the comforts of home, lack of privacy, lack of conversation. Yep, the life of a person in prison is defined by lack.

readingMnemonic: You can’t believe how awful these <kanji>smell</kanji>s are. You’re new in prison, so you call them all <reading>neo</reading>-smells (にお). They're neo, they're new to you.
meaningMnemonic: You're stuck in <radical>prison</radical> with nothing but a <radical>spoon</radical>, and the <kanji>smell</kanji> in here is so bad you’re using the prison spoon to waft it outside as best you can.

This radical looks like a hat with some legs under it. If all you can see is legs, the person wearing the hat must really be <radical>jammed in</radical> there. Have you ever tried to cram yourself into a hat so hard it covers your body? Yeah, didn't think so. But imagine how jammed in to that hat you'd be if you did.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>boat</kanji> <kanji>ship</kanji> is still a <vocabulary>ship</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When your <kanji>self</kanji> has <kanji>overconfidence</kanji> in something, that's called <vocabulary>pride</vocabulary>. You can't shut up about that thing, and you <vocabulary>boast</vocabulary> about it to whoever will listen.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji, except that もち becomes もっ.
meaningMnemonic:
You <kanji>must not</kanji> use your <kanji>body</kanji> for anything <vocabulary>wasteful</vocabulary>, because that would be <vocabulary>a waste</vocabulary>. You're <vocabulary>too good</vocabulary> for that!

This word is used in all kinds of situations where there's a feeling that something is going to waste, including food, money, time, talent, and opportunities. You can also use it to say that someone is too good for a job, or even for another person. While it's usually written in kana, you'll see it in kanji too.

readingMnemonic: <kanji>Congratulate</kanji> the pilot with <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい)!
meaningMnemonic: If a pilot manages to land under a <radical>canopy</radical> with a <radical>helicopter</radical> that's pierced with a sideways <radical>barb</radical> in the <radical>heart</radical> of <radical>winter</radical> you should <kanji>congratulate</kanji> them! People should always be congratulated for doing good things, and this is one of the best things you've ever heard of!

readingMnemonic: The reading is all on'yomi readings, which you learned for all but 花. Instead, 花 is か, and to remember that you can think about how the only way to escape the <vocabulary>hay fever</vocabulary> is to jump in your <reading>ca</reading>r and turn on the filter. Sweet, sweet relief.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>flower</kanji> <kanji>powder</kanji> <kanji>symptom</kanji>s are when you start sneezing from flower powder, aka pollen that comes from all sorts of flowers, which is pretty much all plants. This word, however, refers to the most common version of this sickness, which is <vocabulary>hay fever</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>feeling</kanji> of <kanji>inscription</kanji> is the feeling one gets when something so strong happens that it's like the feeling gets inscribed into your soul. This is something that left a very <vocabulary>deep impression</vocabulary>.
ワンピース comes from the English word one-piece, but it generally refers to a casual <vocabulary>dress</vocabulary> in Japanese.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>writing</kanji> on a <kanji>tombstone</kanji> makes up the <vocabulary>inscription</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>epitaph</vocabulary> the family members decided to put there.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>enter</kanji> your <kanji>supply</kanji> into the machine, that is your <vocabulary>payment</vocabulary> for the day. Every day you have to enter your supply, otherwise they crack down on you.
There's a stick going through some juicy meat. This is a <radical>skewer</radical>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>news report</kanji> that covers things <kanji>beforehand</kanji> (before they happen) is a <vocabulary>forecast</vocabulary>. For example, a weather forecast is a 天気予報.

readingMnemonic: The simple drunkard started a <kanji>war</kanji> with the <reading>cen</reading>taurs (せん)! This is especially unfortunate, because the centaurs are really good at <kanji>battle</kanji>s because they're all automatically cavalry troops.
meaningMnemonic: A <radical>simple</radical> <radical>drunkard</radical> starting a <kanji>war</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: <kanji>Me</kanji>, personally, <kanji>I</kanji> am quite thirsty so I ask for some “<reading>waga</reading>” (わが). I have five things in my mouth, so it is hard for me to pronounce the word “water”. So it sounds like “waga” when I ask for it. “Coulg I pweash hab sum waga?! I deed waga!!”
meaningMnemonic: I have <radical>five</radical> things in my <radical>mouth</radical> and <kanji>I</kanji> need them all for <kanji>me</kanji>. I own these five things, and I keep them in my mouth so people like you cannot take them from me.

readingMnemonic: Now that you know how to figure out what <kanji>day of the week</kanji> it is, you can start making <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). It can take up to 24 hours to make yogurt. Knowing which weekday it is at any given moment means you can perfect your yogurt-making schedule.
meaningMnemonic: When the <radical>sun</radical> is out, you can see two <radical>Wolverine</radical>s and a <radical>turkey</radical> playing together, but only on a certain <kanji>weekday</kanji>. Which <kanji>day of the week</kanji> is it? I'll never tell you. It could be Sunday. It could be Monday. It could be any day of the week.

readingMnemonic:
The reading for this vocab doesn't follow any rules you learned previously. It's an exception, which means you have to learn the reading separately too. Spend a few moments trying to remember this word, look away for 10 seconds, and then try to recall its reading. Could you do it? Try again, this time in thirty seconds. Did you do it again? Okay, go ahead and move on. You may know it now, though you'll need to recall it again in the next 5-10 minutes if you want to remember it for good.

Alternatively, if you know the reading for the vocab word 一つ (in the same level as this word), you can know that it uses the same reading!
meaningMnemonic: When there's <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>, what are they? Well, they're either just going to be simply <vocabulary>one person</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>alone</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

readingMnemonic: You're <vocabulary>busy</vocabulary> because you have to take care of your friend's <reading>ice ogre</reading>s (いそが) this weekend. You don't know why you agreed to this, you were busy enough, but now you'll never get anything done running around taking care of these little ice ogres.
meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with しい on the end, meaning it's an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>busy</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>busy</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>superior</kanji> <kanji>haiku</kanji> requires someone really famous and well known to read it... it's just on that level. Who is super well known and who deserves to read this superior haiku? A great <vocabulary>actor</vocabulary>, perhaps?

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
When you <kanji>preserve</kanji> the things you <kanji>hold</kanji> on to, you're <vocabulary>keep</vocabulary>ing them. In other words, you're <vocabulary>hold</vocabulary>ing and <vocabulary>maintain</vocabulary>ing them!

Note that 保持 is a formal word that's commonly used in professional or official contexts.

readingMnemonic: Since this guy is such a pathetic drunkard, it comes as no <reading>shock</reading> (しょく) that he can’t find <kanji>employment</kanji>. If he did find employment, I would be filled with both shock and awe.
meaningMnemonic: Reaching your <radical>ear</radical> is the <radical>sound</radical> of a <radical>drunkard</radical> who can’t find <kanji>employment</kanji>. You hear him before you see him because he’s behind some trash cans. Being a drunkard, he’s like, super wasted and just kind of rambling to himself, making strange sounds. No wonder he can’t find employment.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Immersed</kanji> in <kanji>water</kanji>. That sounds like <vocabulary>submersion</vocabulary>. Possibly like a <vocabulary>flood</vocabulary>, even.

readingMnemonic:
The reading comes from 握り.

Note that this is usually written in hiragana as おにぎり.
meaningMnemonic: 握り is a "grip." When you add お it's elevated a bit. For some reason it becomes a <vocabulary>rice ball</vocabulary> (aka <vocabulary>onigiri</vocabulary>). To make a rice ball, you use your grip to make them into a ball shape, which is probably where it comes from.

readingMnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the reading you'll be using here. Because of that, this word is kind of a <vocabulary>lightweight</vocabulary>.
meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>lightweight</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>lightweight</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>club</kanji> <kanji>room</kanji> is a <vocabulary>clubroom</vocabulary>!

readingMnemonic: You shoot, but it's <vocabulary>a miss</vocabulary>. Way <vocabulary>off the mark</vocabulary>. Better put on your <reading>haz</reading>mat (はず) suit because you hit a toxic waste barrel instead of the target. Put your hazmat suits on, everyone!
meaningMnemonic:
外れる is "to come off" or "to be off." And this is its noun form — <vocabulary>a miss</vocabulary>, aka something that's <vocabulary>off the mark</vocabulary>. Whatever it is, it's completely off the original goal or intended target.

This word refers to something that falls outside of what's expected, central, or correct. Like something that didn't match your hopes or expectations — a losing lottery ticket or a disappointing purchase. It can also describe a place on the <vocabulary>periphery</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>outskirts</vocabulary> — since you're "off the mark" from somewhere more central.

readingMnemonic: The reading is 兄 on its own plus the reading for 貴. ANIKIIIII.
meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>older brother</kanji> is <kanji>valuable</kanji> to you. But, no matter how valuable he is to you, he's still just your <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary>. 

P.S. You'll often see some gangstah thug call a higher ranking gangstah thug (one that acts like an older brother to all the other gangstah thugs) this. It's like family within the gang.

readingMnemonic:
To remember the reading た we use the word "taco."

Let's start with the kanji meaning: <kanji>many</kanji>. You go outside in the evening (because that's what this kanji is made up of) and are surprised when you're hit by <kanji>many</kanji> <reading>ta</reading>cos (た) flying from the sky. For some reason it's raining tacos, and of course you have no idea why.
meaningMnemonic: How many <radical>evenings</radical> are there? There are <kanji>many</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: You use this <kanji>book counter</kanji> method to count all the books <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ) has in her house. Remember her? She's got, like, a ton of books, but she's just a little girl so she needs some help. That's where your book counter know-how comes in handy.
meaningMnemonic: You use a <radical>bookshelf</radical> as a <kanji>book counter</kanji>. Duh. What, are you gonna count them one by one? Okay, well maybe, but you should count them while they're nice and organized on the shelves. Otherwise counting is going to be a huge pain.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Does being <kanji>obese</kanji> mean you're always <kanji>full</kanji>? Of course not. But clearly that's what the people who coined the Japanese word for <vocabulary>obesity</vocabulary> thought... You can see there are some implicit biases in these kanji!

readingMnemonic: There's hiragana attached to this kanji, which means it's probably the kun'yomi reading (and it is). You've seen the kun'yomi reading via the word 近い. So, as long as you know that word, you should be able to read this one as well.
meaningMnemonic: Because this word ends with an う sound, you can tell it's probably a verb. The kanji portion means <kanji>near</kanji>. The verb version of that is <vocabulary>to draw near</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get close</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to approach</vocabulary>. Essentially, the general idea is that you're getting closer to something. You're becoming more nearby. You're approaching.

Your favorite <vocabulary>author</vocabulary> is also a <reading>sack</reading> <reading>sha</reading>man (さくしゃ). They do all sorts of weird magic involving sacks, and you just love reading about it. Maybe one day, you can become a sack shaman and <vocabulary>writer</vocabulary> yourself.
meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Someone</kanji> who <kanji>make</kanji>s is someone who creates things. Back in the day, a creator like this may have been known as many things, but the big one that stands out is an <vocabulary>author</vocabulary>.

Wondering about the difference between 作者 and 作家? Basically, 作者 just refers to the creator of a particular creative work, such as a book, article, artwork, piece of music, etc., while 作家 refers to someone who creates those things as an occupation.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The とう goes to どう, though. Agh, what a <vocabulary>面倒</vocabulary>.
meaningMnemonic: When you're looking straight into the <kanji>face</kanji> of a <kanji>collapse</kanji> it means <vocabulary>trouble</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>difficulty</vocabulary> coming soon.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to be able to read 可能 as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>possible</kanji> (可能) range of <kanji>gender</kanji> extends beyond two options. It means there's a <vocabulary>possibility</vocabulary> to identify with many different gender identities.

readingMnemonic: Not everyone wants to be <kanji>healthy</kanji>, but <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai sure does. He needs to be ready at a moment's notice so he can do tasks for other people. He's at every class, rubbing himself down with the brush.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of your <radical>yoga</radical> class uses a special <radical>brush</radical> to stay <kanji>healthy</kanji>. She rubs the brush on her long arms and legs, and she never ever gets sick.

readingMnemonic: You've already learned both 町 and 外れ, so just combine the two and you get 町外れ not only in meaning, but also in reading!
meaningMnemonic: You already know that 町 means "town" and that 外れ can mean "periphery" or "outskirts." This is just a combination of the two, so it means the <vocabulary>outskirts of town</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading also comes from 選択.
meaningMnemonic: 選択 is "selection" or "choice." If you do the verb version of this, you are going <vocabulary>to select</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to choose</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Remember how 教育 means "education?" Well, the 育 here is referring to the education word, but this time it's a <kanji>body</kanji> education. What do you call the body education at school? <vocabulary>Physical education</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>PE</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

On <vocabulary>both days</vocabulary> of your vacation, you get two boats to <reading>row</reading>! <reading>Gee, two</reading> (りょうじつ) boats at once? Try not to fall in!
meaningMnemonic:
Kanji doesn't go together much better than this. <kanji>Both</kanji> plus <kanji>day</kanji> equals <vocabulary>both days</vocabulary>.

This is a bit of a formal word though, you'll hear important people say it more than your friends.

Remember how どれ means "which one"? どの has a very similar meaning: <vocabulary>which</vocabulary>. Whereas どれ is used on its own, どの is used before a noun to ask "which" out of three or more options. So for example, どの本 is "which book (out of that pile)?".

Notice how question words often start with a ど? We'll be seeing more of these!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>normal</kanji> <kanji>steps</kanji> are the ones that are totally <vocabulary>usual</vocabulary>. They're the ones you <vocabulary>usually</vocabulary> do, unlike those weird not usual steps.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The thing we <kanji>leave behind</kanji> at a <kanji>fault</kanji> is a <vocabulary>loss</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The readings for the kanji in this word are the kun'yomi readings. Since you've already seen the word 青, hopefully you can just combine it with 葉 (you learned the reading for this part with the kanji). Be sure to pay attention to the rendaku, though. は goes to ば in this word, making it <reading>あおば</reading>.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>young</kanji> <kanji>leaf</kanji> is exactly what you'd expect, although most people usually just call them <vocabulary>fresh leaves</vocabulary>.

Remember how there's some overlap between blue and green in Japanese? 青葉 is another example!  That's why 青 is used to describe fresh and lush green leaves, especially those on trees during early summer.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic:
What's <kanji>above</kanji> the stage and involves <kanji>acting</kanji>? A <vocabulary>performance</vocabulary>!

This word does not refer to an actor's acting on stage. Instead, it usually refers to a theatrical or musical presentation in its entirety, so it's used in contexts relating to the act of staging an artistic or dramatic production, or features of the production itself, like its start time or running time (as in 上演時間).
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>form</radical>.

readingMnemonic: Reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: If you know the reading of the word 長い from level 6 you'll know the reading for this word too. Only difference is the さ at the end, which is hiragana so it should be easy to read.
meaningMnemonic: You know the word 長い from a couple levels ago. This is like the word 大きい versus 大きさ, where 大きさ is "size" and 大きい is "big." So, 長い is "long" and 長さ is <vocabulary>length</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is double kun'yomi. Think of 手紙 as two words mashed together — a letter is a thing you write by hand (て) on paper (かみ). You've learned those readings already, so you should be able to read this! Just watch out for the rendaku on がみ.

A <kanji>hand</kanji> <kanji>paper</kanji> is a <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary> because letters are generally written by hand on paper.

If you want a more graphic image, imagine writing a letter on your hand, and how much it would hurt to chop off your hand and send it.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 刺す.
meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb, meaning that the piercing just happens, without emphasis on what makes it happen. That's why it means <vocabulary>to pierce into</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to stick in</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to stab into</vocabulary>. 

This is a tricky word because its English translations often end up being transitive, but in Japanese we always use this with the particle に, not を, so it's intransitive. You can see this in phrases like 言葉が心に刺さった (the words pierced my heart).

readingMnemonic: Who do you love to <kanji>hug</kanji> the most? Your <reading>da</reading>d (だ)! He gives the best hugs. They're warm and big and tight and comforting. The kind of hug dads are really good at giving.
meaningMnemonic: Take your <radical>fingers</radical> and <radical>wrap</radical> them around another person. This is called a <kanji>hug</kanji>. Just make sure you include all the stuff attached to your fingers, like your hands and arms too, otherwise it's more of a squeeze, and we don't want to do that to people.

初めに has a lot of overlap with 始めに. But while 始めに is for the beginning of some larger process, 初めに refers more to doing something first or to the initial point of a certain time frame. You might say 初めにアクビをしたのは私です (I was the one who yawned first), for example, or 今年の初めに (at the start of this year).

When you have a "feeling" (気持ち) that is "good" (いい), you are <vocabulary>feeling good</vocabulary>.

Whenever you try <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary> something, you just start screaming "<reading>WAAAAAAAAAHHHH</reading>" (わ). It helps you focus and concentrate on what you’re trying to understand, to the dismay of everyone around you. WAAAAAAAAAHHHH.
meaningMnemonic:

Watch out, though, because whereas in English you understand something, in Japanese the thing you understand is the grammatical subject (it's doing the action). So, a more literal meaning for this is <vocabulary>to be understandable</vocabulary>. In other words, there's no object, and 分かる is intransitive, meaning it happens on its own. The かる ending is a hint, because verbs with かる as okurigana (kana added to the kanji) are usually intransitive.

It gets bright each morning when a new day dawns, so the connection kinda makes sense, right?

While 明ける is commonly used with 夜 to talk about the dawn breaking, it's also often used to talk about other time-related transitions. Because of this, it can mean <vocabulary>to end</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> depending on the situation, as in 冬休みが明ける (winter vacation ends) or 年が明ける (the new year begins). Think of it like a new phase in your life is "dawning."

This one is a little tricky to understand and translate well. At its core, this verb describes the act of arranging all of the necessary things for something. But it can also describe aligning certain things in a uniform, matching manner. If this still isn't clear, have a careful look at our context sentences and collocations!

Think of it this way: you only renew stuff that's not new, after time has worn on a bit — your streaming subscriptions, your driver's license, your marriage vows. And with each renewal you feel the passage of time a little more deeply… You'll see 更ける more often in writing, usually in reference to night or autumn, as in 夜が更ける (the night grows late) and 秋が更ける (autumn deepens).

Remember how あれ means "that one over there"? Well, あの means <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>, and goes before a noun to point out something that is far away from both you and the person you're talking to, such as あの本 (that book over there) or あの子犬 (that puppy over there).

Notice how these words starting with あ are far away from you? We'll be learning a few more of these, and they all follow the same pattern! What's more, you’ll notice that words ending in の tend to go before a noun.

readingMnemonic: You love to <kanji>fry</kanji> things and are also an adventurous <reading>eater</reading> (いた). This means you'll fry and eat just about anything. Fried ostrich, fried alligator, fried chocolate, you name it!
meaningMnemonic: <radical>Fire</radical> is one of a <radical>few</radical> things you'll need to <kanji>fry</kanji> things.

readingMnemonic: The reason you are interested in these <kanji>revered</kanji> horns so much is that your <reading>son</reading> (そん) is sick and you need one of these revered horns to make a medicine for your son. Only with the revered power of the horns will you be able to save your son’s life.

The horns are revered both for their size and potency. The horns can be used in medicine, so they are very valuable, those alcoholic monster horns.

readingMnemonic:
What are you going <vocabulary>to embrace</vocabulary>? How about your <reading>da</reading>d (だ)? Or if he's not around, maybe an <reading>e</reading>-<reading>da</reading>d (いだ)? You know, like a digital version of a dad.

The two readings for this word have different nuances. だく is more for physical holding and hugging, as in 赤ちゃんを抱く (to hold a baby). But when it's something you hold in your heart, like an emotion or feeling, use the いだく reading: 疑問を抱く (to hold doubts) or 夢を抱く (to have a dream), for example.
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hug</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to embrace</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hold</vocabulary> (in one's arms, that is). It can also mean <vocabulary>to hug</vocabulary>, especially in the form of 抱きしめる.

Keep in mind that depending on the context, 抱く can be a euphemism for something way more sexual than just hugging. Not always, of course, but pretty often, so just be careful how you use it! 抱きしめる is the better option if you're talking about regular old hugs.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: This vocab word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji. At least I won't have to bring up the image of you <reading>moon</reading>ing (むね) people with your breasts or whatnot. Oh dang, I just went and did it.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you manage to make <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>part</kanji>s of something work together you worked <vocabulary>very</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>extremely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>considerably</vocabulary> hard to do it. Doing all of anything is hard so lots of work had to happen.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Continue to think you're driving on this road. You hit something, then look <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary> you, seeing you hit a cow. Know the word for cow in Japanese? It's うし, which is also the reading for this word.
