While 後で (you may or may not have seen this word yet) means "after," this one means all the other meanings you learned with the kanji: <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>back</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>rear</vocabulary>. Think of the ろ as a hint. It's like saying you're on the "road" (ろ) and you're driving so fast you're leaving everything "behind."

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Both kanji have a couple different on'yomi readings though, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember which ones to pick:

Your <vocabulary>arch enemy</vocabulary> is the <reading>tie techie</reading> (たいてき). Who's the tie techie? He's the tech support guy at work who always wears the same tie and never helps you. He just says "try restarting your computer" to every problem, which isn't helpful. He's not just a great enemy, he's basically your nemesis. You hate that tie techie.
meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>enemy</kanji> is your worst enemy. Your <vocabulary>arch enemy</vocabulary>.

大敵 is for a powerful or dangerous opponent, whether it's a <vocabulary>formidable adversary</vocabulary> in battle or competition, or something abstract, like calling carelessness your <vocabulary>great enemy</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

<kanji>Send back</kanji> to the <kanji>origin</kanji> means you are going to <vocabulary>give something back</vocabulary>. This word is commonly used to mean "giving benefits back to the consumers.” For example, if a company makes more money than usual, they can thank consumers with a 利益還元 sale, lowering prices to "give back" some of the profits.

In the context of chemistry, 還元 also means <vocabulary>reduction</vocabulary>, like reducing an oxidized substance back to its original, unoxidized form.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well, but just remember that the second kanji is read as ぱい because of the rendaku on はい.
meaningMnemonic: My <kanji>comrade</kanji> who came <kanji>before</kanji> me is my <vocabulary>senior</vocabulary>, my senpai (せんぱい).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: Express your unique <kanji>idea</kanji> of <kanji>condolence</kanji> by offering your <vocabulary>condolence</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>sympathy</vocabulary> to people who are going through hard times.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You might remember the on'yomi for 様 from the vocab 〜の様に, but here's a mnemonic for it just in case:

You see a <vocabulary>pattern</vocabulary> in your <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). Could this be a divine message? Or maybe this yogurt is just way past its expiration date. Either way, a pattern in your yogurt is something you ought to pay attention to.

readingMnemonic: You're killing this turkey, and you need to make sure he's dead for <kanji>certain</kanji>. The reason you need to make sure this turkey is dead is because of the <reading>cock</reading> (かく) in your life. Male chickens get really jealous when turkeys are around.

This radical is a <radical>cage</radical> because it's covered on all sides but one (the one open side is where the cage door or gate is). There's nothing inside this cage because there's no gate, and whatever was inside has gotten out. I hope it wasn't rabid...

readingMnemonic: The only way to stop the <kanji>chicken</kanji> from putting on your husband's cleats and stepping on him to death in revenge is to feed it the <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい) you were making.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Be careful of the shortening, and don't be tricked by the hiragana sticking out. The readings of the kanji don't change.

This word can also mean <vocabulary>annoying</vocabulary>. If something or someone always makes you feel gloomy, you'll probably think it's annoying, right?

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>month</kanji>'s <kanji>amount</kanji> is the <vocabulary>monthly amount</vocabulary>.

Instead of one husband and one wife, we have two husbands here. They shed their lives of bachelorhood and replace it with one of monogamy.

You don't want this here, so you decide to <kanji>send back</kanji> the zombie. (It's a weird zombie because it has the ground on top of its head instead of dirt!)

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Hide</kanji> your <kanji>name</kanji> for <vocabulary>anonymity</vocabulary>. There's lots of that here on the internet. readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: What is the greatest <kanji>art</kanji> a <kanji>person</kanji> can possess? It’s got to be the art of making people laugh. That’s why this means <vocabulary>comedian</vocabulary>, though it can also mean a <vocabulary>performer</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>entertainer</vocabulary> more generally.

readingMnemonic: Dealing with the <kanji>passage of time</kanji> can be tough, so after you tie the thread to the tombstone, each year you eat a piece of <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい). You already eat cake to mark the passage of time on your birthday, so why not here as well?
meaningMnemonic: Tying a <radical>thread</radical> to a <radical>tombstone</radical> each year will help you <kanji>manage</kanji> the <kanji>passage of time</kanji>. That way you’ll know how many years you <kanji>pass through</kanji>, since you’ll have one thread for each year to count.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>write down</kanji> a lot of stuff focusing on one <kanji>thing</kanji> it's called an <vocabulary>article</vocabulary>. If it's on something that just happened it will probably be a <vocabulary>news story</vocabulary>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>oversee</radical>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that 世 is せ here, and not せい!
meaningMnemonic: Older <kanji>generation</kanji>s mostly <kanji>talk</kanji> about one thing: <vocabulary>care</vocabulary>. Everybody wants to receive care once they're older, don't they?

This might remind you of 米, which has three stalks sprouting upward. You can tell the difference because the top of this one is slanted from the weight of the ripe grain.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>patrol</kanji>, but what do you do when you patrol? You go around, which is <vocabulary>to go around</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just watch out for ふ becoming ぷ.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this on your own.

It allows you to have some <vocabulary>restraint</vocabulary>, since your considerations are far from here. It also allows you to <vocabulary>decline</vocabulary> things, since you're not considering the other person's feelings.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi reading for the first kanji and the kun'yomi reading for the second kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this too!
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>heart</kanji> <kanji>bottom</kanji> is the <vocabulary>bottom of one's heart</vocabulary>. Do you want to learn kanji? Do you want to learn it from 心底? Okay, fine, you can move onto the reading then.

readingMnemonic: What a selfish kid, right? Well, all he thinks about is "<reading>Me</reading> (み) me me me me me me me me me me." Hate kids like that.
meaningMnemonic: You're flying in a <radical>jet</radical>. Even though it's one of the fastest things on earth, your child is sitting in the back asking, "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" You have to keep responding. "<kanji>Not yet</kanji>! Not yet! NOT YET!"

readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for the first kanji and the on'yomi reading for the second. You've learned both of the readings, so you should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>evening</kanji> <kanji>edition</kanji> is the <vocabulary>evening edition</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Just <vocabulary>ahead</vocabulary> of you are the <vocabulary>tip</vocabulary>s of a <reading>saw</reading> and a <reading>key</reading>(さき). You have no idea what they're doing there, but both saws and keys have very sharp tips, so watch out you don't hurt yourself. Imagine yourself edging carefully past those saw and key tips.

You can differentiate this from 先ず (まず) because it doesn't have any hiragana on the end.
meaningMnemonic:
Everything that happened to you <kanji>previous</kanji>ly is just the <vocabulary>tip</vocabulary> of the iceberg, and the important stuff is <vocabulary>ahead</vocabulary> of you, in your <vocabulary>future</vocabulary>. So make sure you put that stuff <vocabulary>first</vocabulary>!

The original meaning of this word is the tip of something, like a pen or a finger. From that meaning, it's expanded into all sorts of meanings, like ahead, first, and future, depending on the context and where it is in the sentence. It can also mean "previous" in formal contexts (and we'll accept that meaning too, but we're not teaching it here because it's more advanced).

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi of both kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

What's the best way for your servants <vocabulary>to make an offering</vocabulary>? When they <vocabulary>offer</vocabulary> up their sauna (そな)! You really value a warm and relaxing sauna session at the end of the day.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>offer</kanji>, and this verb version means <vocabulary>to make an offering</vocabulary>.

供える means <vocabulary>to offer</vocabulary> something, usually to a god, Buddha, or someone who has passed away. For example, you might 花を供える (offer flowers) at a grave or altar.

readingMnemonic: While wolverine <kanji>sleep</kanji>s, he makes a horrible <reading>neigh</reading>ing (ね) sound. It's like there's a giant horse in his mouth screaming to get out! NEIGH NEIGH!
meaningMnemonic: From the <radical>roof</radical>, an <radical>icicle</radical> falls and hits <radical>Wolverine</radical> in the <radical>forehead</radical>, and he has to go over to the <radical>stool</radical> to <kanji>lie down</kanji>. And eventually he goes to <kanji>sleep</kanji>.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Don't have to use your <vocabulary>brain</vocabulary> for that.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic:
With your arms <kanji>spread</kanji> like that, you look extremely <reading>chic</reading> (しき). Spread arms are obviously a chic posture, and the fact that you're holding a cross makes it even more chic. 

Side note: The official kun'yomi reading is just し, but since far more words use しき, we're focusing on that here. Even though the き part is technically okurigana, it's actually used in the readings for most of the compounds that use this kanji!
meaningMnemonic: Taking a <radical>cross</radical> with a <radical>drop</radical> on it, you walk through the <radical>rice paddy</radical> in the <radical>direction</radical> of <radical>winter</radical> and <kanji>spread</kanji> your arms wide. You spread your arms to halt the approach of winter because your rice paddy is not done growing yet. You take the cross with you for some extra religious power of persuasion, and the drop in case any of that rice is thirsty.

readingMnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi of 内緒 and kun'yomi of 話, only rendakued.
meaningMnemonic: Remember how 内緒 means "secret" or "confidential"? Well, that makes this is a secret <kanji>talk</kanji>, aka a <vocabulary>confidential talk</vocabulary> — like the kind often done by <vocabulary>whispering</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you're <kanji>solemn</kanji> by your<kanji>self</kanji>, you have a lot of <vocabulary>self control</vocabulary>. You don't need anyone to tell you to be that way, you have your own <vocabulary>self discipline</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: What are you conceding? Some delicious <reading>yuzu</reading> (ゆず). You are sad, because they're so much better than lemons and now you don't have them.
meaningMnemonic: If you are going to <kanji>defer</kanji> to someone, you are going <vocabulary>to concede</vocabulary> something. I concede / defer this to you.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. It's also the same as the meaning of the kanji / vocab, though you can think of this as <vocabulary> Japanese plum</vocabulary> as well if you want.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: If you <kanji>dry up</kanji> syrup like this, you're removing its <reading>sou</reading>l (そう). Have you ever seen dry syrup before? No soul in that. In fact, you probably have no soul if you can dry out syrup like this without feeling bad about it.
meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>fire</radical> next to which you left some <radical>syrup</radical>, and it has all <kanji>dried up</kanji>! 触れる is often for when something happens <vocabulary>to come into contact with</vocabulary> something, possibly in a fleeting or momentary way. It's still used in phrases like "When I touched your hand," but has a lighter, more indirect and literary feel than 触る, which conveys a greater sense of purpose and intent behind the action.

触れる is often used in constructions like 手がカバンに触れる (one's hand touches a bag), where が indicates what's doing the touching and に marks what's being touched. If you see を instead of が, 触れる becomes transitive, changing the meaning to "to have your hand touch a bag."

There's a <radical>tsunami</radical> coming and you can't <radical>stop</radical> the <radical>explosion</radical> of <kanji>bitter</kanji>ness in your mouth. You're scared. Your mouth tastes bitter and <kanji>astringent</kanji>.

This word also means <kanji>reluctant</kanji>, because wouldn't you be reluctant to let a tsunami come wash you away with that bitter explosion of flavor in your mouth?

readingMnemonic: The readings are the vocab words お金 and 儲ける combined together into one. As long as you remember the readings of those words, you should be able to read this one too.
meaningMnemonic:
The 金 here is from お金 (money), and you recently learned that 儲ける is "to make a profit." Well, if you're acquiring money and making a profit, you are <vocabulary>making money</vocabulary>. You've got this whole <vocabulary>money-making</vocabulary> thing figured out.

金儲け is a casual word for making money with a practical and slightly self-interested vibe. It's direct and a tad rough — the kind of term you'd hear in unvarnished talk about profit, side hustles, and get-rich-quick schemes.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>point</kanji> at which something starts to <kanji>boil</kanji> is the <vocabulary>boiling point</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: One tree? No. Two trees? Not enough. I want <reading>more</reading> (もり) trees, please!
meaningMnemonic: This kanji is just the <radical>tree</radical> radical three times. Just based off this, you should be able to figure it out. This kanji means "<kanji>forest</kanji>."

readingMnemonic: So what did you receive as a <kanji>thanks</kanji>? You open it up, and there's a <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun inside!
meaningMnemonic: What do you get if you lend a <radical>spirit</radical> your <radical>umbrella</radical>? <kanji>Thanks</kanji>, of course! Especially if that spirit is Totoro, the spirit of the forest.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>period of time</kanji> <kanji>limit</kanji> is the <vocabulary>deadline</vocabulary> for a certain thing. Alternatively, this can describe a <vocabulary>term</vocabulary> for something, like the repayment of debts, or some sort of <vocabulary>due date</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know the word 出版 as well, though.
meaningMnemonic: If 出版 means <kanji>publishing</kanji>, then a <kanji>company</kanji> that does said publishing is a <vocabulary>publishing company</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. One thing to note though:

This word uses the かい reading for 街 (not がい). And even when 街道 is a suffix, it never gets rendaku'd! Remember this by imagining an olden-day <vocabulary>highway</vocabulary> full of people in <reading>kay</reading>aks (かい). You know, the horse-drawn kayaks people would use to travel long distances before the invention of cars. You've heard of those, right?
meaningMnemonic:
When <kanji>streets</kanji> and <kanji>road</kanji>s are combined together, you get something wide enough to be a <vocabulary>highway</vocabulary>!

But 街道 doesn't mean a modern highway that you drive on. It refers to the great <vocabulary>high road</vocabulary>s of the past that linked major cities and regions. In Japan, these were typically the Edo-period routes like 日光街道 (Nikkō Kaidō) and 中山道 (Nakasendō). It also works for other historically important routes, like ancient Rome's アッピア街道 (the Appian Way).

readingMnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading for 場 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

At the <vocabulary>boarding area</vocabulary>, you <reading>baa</reading> (ば) at the bus driver to ask if this is the right bus. You're in a country inhabited only by sheep, but luckily you've practiced your Sheepanese well enough to be able to baa for directions at <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>s, <vocabulary>taxi stand</vocabulary>s, and <vocabulary>train platform</vocabulary>s.
meaningMnemonic: What's a <kanji>ride</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji>? It's a <vocabulary>boarding area</vocabulary>! This word is used widely to refer to any place where you board transportation, such as a <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>taxi stand</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>train platform</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>cruel</kanji> <kanji>cool</kanji> person is more <vocabulary>cruel</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>coldhearted</vocabulary> than just a normal cruel person. It's probably because they're cold all the time and it makes them mad. You should stay away from people like that.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which means it uses on'yomi readings for both of the kanji. You already know those, so you should be good to go!
meaningMnemonic:
When you buy something, you basically <kanji>substitute</kanji> it with <kanji>money</kanji>. That substitute money is the <vocabulary>cost</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>price</vocabulary> of the thing you're paying for.

There are a lot of money-related synonyms in Japanese, but keep in mind this one refers to the money you pay to get some stuff in return (usually goods), not to an expense, price, or value. It's "substitute money" after all!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>pressure</kanji> <kanji>power</kanji> is the <vocabulary>pressure</vocabulary>. This can also be <vocabulary>stress</vocabulary> as well.

readingMnemonic: The reading is たい for 台, which is a little different from what you learned, but not the end of the world (especially if you can get the meaning down). The わん is however what you learned, so even if you arrive to だいわん, you'll probably realize that this is たいわん.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>machine</kanji> <kanji>gulf</kanji> isn't what you'd expect. In fact, looking at the reading will probably help the most first, since this word represents <vocabulary>Taiwan</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: If your name is in a <kanji>register</kanji>, people will find you very <reading>sexy</reading> (せき). This was true long ago too. There's nothing sexier than someone whose existence is accounted for in official documentation.
meaningMnemonic: People had to use their <radical>bamboo</radical> <radical>plow</radical>s <radical>long ago</radical> to put their name in a <kanji>register</kanji>. This is because there was no paper yet, so they would hitch a cow to their bamboo plow, and dig their names into the dirt to create all kinds of registers.

readingMnemonic: You weren't expecting to see such a <kanji>mediocre</kanji> table so you go up to the guy who's selling it and say, "Hey, I have a <reading>bone</reading> (ぼん) to pick with you!" But he doesn't think there is a bone to pick at all, he doesn't think the table is mediocre like you do.
meaningMnemonic: You go to buy a <radical>table</radical> but it looks like it has water damage from <radical>drop</radical>s of water hitting it. This makes it a pretty <kanji>mediocre</kanji> table. The water drops haven't really damaged it that much, it still stands and you can use it, but it's kinda ugly, so it's just mediocre.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When you are given <kanji>superior</kanji> <kanji>treatment</kanji> it's called <vocabulary>preferential treatment</vocabulary>. This is the best way to be treated.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: 原 is often tied to atomic things, as atoms are the origin of all things. If an atom <kanji>explode</kanji>s, you have yourself an <vocabulary>atomic bomb</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: The readings are the vocab readings of the individual kanji. For 髪 that's no problem. For 型 just remember that it's the individual vocab reading. Watch out for the rendaku.
meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>hair</kanji> <kanji>model</kanji> is how you model your hair. It's your <vocabulary>hairstyle</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hairdo</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 幕 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you try to peek through the <vocabulary>bakufu</vocabulary>'s curtain you'll only see someone's <reading>back</reading> (ばく). They all huddle together to discuss things so a row of hunched backs is all you'll get out of the shogunate. That's not helpful.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>government</kanji> behind a <kanji>curtain</kanji> is the <vocabulary>bakufu</vocabulary>. They didn't let anyone know their government secrets so they would hide behind that curtain and keep everything to themselves.

readingMnemonic: The <kanji>plan</kanji> that made this hat stop right in its tracks was very simple. First, obtain the <reading>key</reading> (き) to the house. Then, use the key to get in the front door. How simple!
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>hat</radical> comes to a <radical>stop</radical>, thinking of a <kanji>plan</kanji>. The hat had been pacing around for a while, trying to think of how to get off the head he's resting upon and back into the house where it's nice and cozy, and came to the sudden realization of a plan. This caused the hat to stop.

readingMnemonic: This is a verb, so it uses the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you already learned this with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!
meaningMnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>come true</kanji>, and this is the intransitive verb version of that, making this <vocabulary>to come true</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be fulfilled</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: If you want to <kanji>look at</kanji> and give a quick <kanji>inspection</kanji> of some stuff then you're just <vocabulary>browsing</vocabulary>. You don't want to buy yet, you just have to give a look.
This radical swings like a monkey, howls like a wolf, and pounces like a leopard. You can almost hear the jungle chorus… This is the radical for <radical>animal</radical>!

readingMnemonic: You realized that the only way to <kanji>cure</kanji> the Death Star is to turn it back into a <reading>yu</reading>rt (ゆ). Then it won't be able to do any more harm, and its outside will reflect its pleasant self on the inside!

meaningMnemonic: Someone with <kanji>bad</kanji> <kanji>energy</kanji> is someone who has <vocabulary>evil intent</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>malice</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>ill will</vocabulary>. Hopefully you don't have too much 悪気.

You can use your strength <vocabulary>to let something fly</vocabulary>, and that something is a <reading>bus</reading> (ばす). You're that buff!
meaningMnemonic: Remember how 飛ぶ is to fly? Well this word is for when you make some thing fly. So, this word is <vocabulary>to let something fly</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to send something flying</vocabulary>. It also means <vocabulary>to skip over something</vocabulary>, such as someone's turn or a question on a test.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: This is a combination of the words 家庭 and 教師. A "teacher" who only teaches when you're with your "family" is known as a <vocabulary>tutor</vocabulary>. They don't teach you at school, they're a <vocabulary>private teacher</vocabulary> that comes to your home to help you learn.

readingMnemonic: The person on this planet with two suns who benefits from the prosperity the most is the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). Yes, this planet still has a shougun as their leader, but everything is going so well that they didn't see a need to change. The shogun will be in charge of this prosperous world forever. No one ever thinks of revolt when everyone has everything they could ever need.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is the reason why crops grow and people can get out of bed in the morning. But on planets with two <radical>sun</radical>s, they can get even more done and it makes them way more <kanji>prosperous</kanji> than us. They work all day, then as the first sun sets, the second one rises and they get a new burst of energy. The whole planet lives in a state of <kanji>prosperity</kanji> because of the two suns.

readingMnemonic: Uh-oh, it looks like this axe <kanji>soldier</kanji> was so excited about chopping the fins off his fish that he didn't think about how he was going to cook them. The only thing nearby to light on fire is a bale of <reading>hay</reading> (へい). Well, it's not the best thing, but at least it will get these fish cooked.
meaningMnemonic: When you swing your <radical>axe</radical>, the <radical>ground</radical> ends up covered in <radical>fins</radical>, because you're a <kanji>soldier</kanji>. Only a skilled axe soldier could make such precise cuts as to de-fin a bunch of fish like that.

readingMnemonic: Remember the vocab word 〜才 which also meant "<kanji>years old</kanji>"? Well, this has the same reading: さい.
meaningMnemonic: You have to <radical>stop</radical> keeping <radical>canine</radical>s which are <radical>small</radical> once you reach a certain number of <kanji>years old</kanji>. You'll be hitting that age limit this <kanji>year</kanji>, which means your <kanji>time</kanji> with your small canine will end and you'll have to grow up and get a bigger one.

readingMnemonic: That <kanji>mosquito</kanji> noise sounds like it's driving a tiny <reading>ca</reading>r (か) in your ear. How are you supposed to write with a bug driving around going bzzz bzzz like a revving car?

You're trying to write, when you hear that horrible high-pitched mosquito noise in your ear. You jerk your head and swat and it's gone. But when you look down, there's lines all over what you were writing.

readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

This radical looks like a fancy composite <radical>bow</radical> people would use to shoot at targets and definitely not any normal living animals. See how the middle part is being pulled back? Imagine holding this bow and firing it at a target shaped like a giant alligator-crab monster.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>task</kanji> is to open this pickle <kanji>container</kanji>. Why you? Because you are so <vocabulary>dextrous</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>skillful</vocabulary> when it comes to opening pickles.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: You're <kanji>cool</kanji> and <kanji>quiet</kanji>. That's you, daddio. Nice and <vocabulary>cool-headed</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>calm</vocabulary>. So much <vocabulary>composure</vocabulary>

readingMnemonic: You decide white light is the ultimate color. You decide you want to put it on <kanji>all</kanji> things to make everything white. "What a great idea," you think. You try to put it on everything and you nearly succeed... except, the <reading>miners</reading> (みな). They keep getting dirty doing all their mining things. NOOO, your plan is ruined!
meaningMnemonic: If you <radical>compare</radical> <radical>white</radical> light to the other colors you'll realize... white consists of <kanji>all</kanji> the colors in one. It contains all the colors in the spectrum in one color. It is the one color that is <kanji>everything</kanji>.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>business</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You have spikes growing out of a sheep with fins. Turn this thing into a business! You could totally charge people money to look at it. Sure, you could also donate it to science, but a business-minded person like you knows a business opportunity when you see one. Step right up! Just five dollars for a glance at the rare spiky mer-sheep!

readingMnemonic: You've been <kanji>tranquilize</kanji>d and now drool is running down your <reading>chin</reading> (ちん). It's actually really gross. But you don't care, look at all this gold! No one will care about your chin when you're rich!
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>reality</radical> of <radical>gold</radical> is that it has the power to <kanji>tranquilize</kanji> anyone who gets their hands on it. Gold may seem cool to have in movies and songs, but in reality, it has the power to mess you up!

readingMnemonic: What is getting <vocabulary>spread out</vocabulary>? <reading>Shee</reading>p (し)! Someone's been hunting sheep, because you're looking at a bunch of empty (dead) sheep bodies spread out on the ground.
meaningMnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>spread</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to spread out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to lay out</vocabulary>.

This word generally refers to laying something flat, like a carpet or a picnic blanket. This use also extends to laying railroad tracks or asphalt for street paving. Metaphorically, it describes laying down something foundational, like establishing rules or specific organizational systems.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: This is like your <kanji>side</kanji> <kanji>part of speech</kanji>, as in, you add it to the side of a verb because it's an <vocabulary>adverb</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: What do you wear on your <kanji>foot</kanji>? You wear a <reading>sock</reading> (そく).
meaningMnemonic:
The radical for <radical>foot</radical> and the kanji for <kanji>foot</kanji> are exactly the same.

That said, there's another meaning you should keep in mind, which is <kanji>sufficient</kanji>. If you think about it, one foot should be sufficient enough to walk around with. You'd have to hop, but one foot is definitely still sufficient.

readingMnemonic: What <kanji>simultaneously</kanji> protects and kills? Your holy blue <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい).
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>simultaneous</radical> radical and the <kanji>simultaneous</kanji> kanji are the same!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>slice</kanji> <kanji>kill</kanji> is a <vocabulary>killing with a sword</vocabulary>. You don't want to hear this, if at all possible.

readingMnemonic:

meaningMnemonic: When you're talking about some <kanji>other</kanji> <kanji>place</kanji> you're talking about <vocabulary>another place</vocabulary>.

meaningMnemonic: I bet you can guess that フランス means "France." So what happens when you add <kanji>language</kanji> to it? You get the "France Language" aka the <vocabulary>French Language</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>announce</kanji> something to <kanji>warn</kanji> somebody, you're <vocabulary>warning</vocabulary> them. Sometimes you're just trying to give them some helpful <vocabulary>advice</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic:

This is a magic <vocabulary>root</vocabulary> that turns you into a horse. You take a bite and let out a loud <reading>neigh</reading> (ね)!
meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's the case for this word too, which means you should already know how to read this word.
meaningMnemonic: What happens when you have ten five times? You get <vocabulary>fifty</vocabulary>!

readingMnemonic: The 下 uses the alternative reading of げ but 巻 is all good and normal.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>scroll</kanji> that's <kanji>below</kanji> is the last scroll you read, making it the <vocabulary>last volume</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: You need this <kanji>gun</kanji> so you can steal some <reading>jew</reading>els (じゅう)! Why didn't you just use your gold to buy the jewels, you ask? Because! That's not how we did things in olden days. When you want jewels you buy a gun with gold and rob a jewelry store!
meaningMnemonic: Take some <radical>gold</radical> and <radical>allocate</radical> it to buy a <kanji>gun</kanji>. Guns are weapons of the old world, so you can't just buy them with paper money. Guns have to be bought with gold coins or bricks.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: A 距離 is a <kanji>distance</kanji> and 近 is <kanji>near</kanji>. A near distance is a <vocabulary>short distance</vocabulary>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
When your <kanji>purchase</kanji> <kanji>enter</kanji>s into effect, you have made your <vocabulary>purchase</vocabulary>.

購入 is a relatively formal word for the act of purchasing something.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>famous</kanji> <kanji>place</kanji> is a <vocabulary>famous place</vocabulary>. When traveling around Japan, you should ask about the 名所 if you can.

readingMnemonic: The reading for 音 is the 音読み. 読み uses the kun'yomi, though, strangely. Way to mess up the one word that should be all on'yomi, Japan. Way. To. Go.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>sound</kanji> <kanji>read</kanji>ing. What could this be...? Wait a sec, think to Japanese and kanji. What's the reading that uses sounds from another place, specifically China? That's the <vocabulary>Chinese reading</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>on'yomi</vocabulary>. Sounds familiar?

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>fire</kanji> <kanji>disaster</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fire disaster</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>conflagration</vocabulary>.

火災 is a more formal version of 火事. It usually refers to a serious and significant fire that causes extensive damage or loss of life.

readingMnemonic: You need to protect what you <kanji>write down</kanji> and <kanji>record</kanji> for yourself with a <reading>key</reading> (き). These are your special thoughts and feelings, you don't want anyone else to see! Lock them away with a key!
meaningMnemonic: What you <radical>say</radical> to <radical>oneself</radical> (yourself), you decide to <kanji>write down</kanji>. Whether this is in the form of a journal, diary, or blog, you feel the need to <kanji>record</kanji> these important thoughts in some way.

readingMnemonic: Both the kanji in this word use the kun'yomi, which you learned when you learned the vocabulary. When it uses this reading, it sounds casual, and is common in conversation. It can also be read using the on'yomi, though, in which case it has a more formal feel to it. That's typical of on'yomi, which tends to add formality to a word!

readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 歳 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

There's one <vocabulary>year-end gift</vocabulary> that always makes people happy: a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). Who wouldn't be stoked to get a saber as an end-of-year gift? It might be a little tricky to wrap, though…
meaningMnemonic:
Here, 歳 means <kanji>year</kanji> and 暮 comes from 暮れる (to end). So 歳暮 literally means "end of the year," but in modern Japanese, this almost always refers to a <vocabulary>year-end gift</vocabulary>, which is basically a way to say thanks before the year wraps up.

歳暮 is almost always used with the honorific お, as in お歳暮. It's a formal gift, like nicely-wrapped boxed sweets or coffee sent to bosses, clients, or people who have helped you during the year.

readingMnemonic: You take the <kanji>glassy</kanji> rocket and try to stuff some thin <reading>reed</reading>s (り) inside to support it. But because it's clear and glassy the king sees them at the last second.
meaningMnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> wants you to make a <radical>rocket</radical> that looks <kanji>glassy</kanji>. It won't be very stable, and it probably won't work, but making it glassy and pretty is the only way to make the king approve.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Someone is telling you <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary>. They are saying "<reading>you go</reading> (うご) over there. Move! Move!" If it helps, have them pronounce "You go" more like "Ugo."
meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>move</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary>.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>sky</radical>.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.
meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>gentle</kanji> <kanji>path</kanji> is, surprisingly, <vocabulary>judo</vocabulary>. Yep, the sport / art based on throwing people around.

This is the radical for <radical>south</radical>. See how it's pointing south? You can think of the cross on top as a compass rose, and the arrow below (that ¥-looking part) as pointing down south. It's a compass pointing nowhere but south!

readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 華やか. Note the second はな becomes ばな, to be <reading>はなばな</reading>しい.
meaningMnemonic: 華やか is "showy." Now we're doubling it, making it doubly showy. If you make something showy enough, it becomes <vocabulary>gorgeous</vocabulary>, but it also becomes pretty <vocabulary>flamboyant</vocabulary>. So, so, so flamboyant.

readingMnemonic: You know all the readings for this vocab already, just make sure to use the kun'yomi ones!
meaningMnemonic:
While a <kanji>dance</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji> can be a location in which you dance, this word actually means <vocabulary>landing</vocabulary> (as in, a landing between two flights of stairs on a staircase) or <vocabulary>plateau</vocabulary> (as in, for example, a plateauing economy) most of the time.

While the meaning has changed over time to mostly refer to landings on staircases, it can still be used to mean <vocabulary>dance hall</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>dance floor</vocabulary>, although loanwords like ダンスホール are more commonly used these days.

meaningMnemonic:

And just so you know, this is a very formal word used when you're trying to be polite. So keep that in mind, please!

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: You learned this reading of 紫 when you learned the kanji, so you should be good to go!

readingMnemonic: You're being really <kanji>gentle</kanji> to the tree when a <reading>jewel</reading> (じゅう) falls out of its branches and hits you on the head.

readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help:

You are moving your lawsuit forward against Sue. But now she says that YOU'RE the problem. "<reading>Sue, sue me</reading>," (すすめ) you say as you continue to advance the lawsuit. Make sure to say "me" like "mehh," in a really snobbish way.
meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>advance</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to advance something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to move something forward</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, so you act upon something else. You advance something. You move something forward. Like a school project, or your plans for taking over the world.

readingMnemonic: You have to be <kanji>gentle</kanji> and handle these things <kanji>gently</kanji> because they belong to <reading>Jo</reading>-Anne (じょ). You're loitering around her surplus of (whatever you decided to imagine).

readingMnemonic: As you stare at the slide <kanji>grid</kanji> you see some people come out and overhear them talk about their mass <reading>maths</reading> (ます) tournament happening later today. Oohhh it IS a giant grid. And they're going to use it to do maths later!
